utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jelic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Cepic will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of the evidence yesterday continues to apply to your evidence today. There's just one matter before we proceed. I should have checked with Mr. Hannis. Time scale for production of the transcript. I think you're able to confirm that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We had discussions with your legal officer yesterday and Mr. Reid, and we believe we should be able to have that by the close of business next Thursday or else sometime on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it's not necessary for us to make an order in view of that information. We are allowing you to produce it by the end of next week. Mr. Bakrac isn't there, but, Mr. Cepic, we indicated that if the production of this transcript should give rise to the need for you to seek to recall any witness, then we would consider such an application. We would require such an application to be made within 14 days after you receive the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please pass that information to Mr. Bakrac when you next see him. And now please proceed with your own examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do that as soon as I finish with this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Great. General, Racak, the 15th of February, 1999, quite a bit was said about that. Was this a joint action of the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period that you are talking about - that is to say, the period that related to Racak - was not a joint action of the army and the police. In actual fact, the army did not take part in it at all and did not enter the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Whose action was Racak, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the knowledge and information I received from the chief of the SUP of Orahovac, this was a purely anti-terrorist action of the MUP forces of the Republic of Serbia searching for terrorist who is had a few days before that fatally wounded a few MUP members.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Exhibit number 5D1377, please. I hope that we have a translation of this document. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, do you see the document in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the command of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. It is being sent to the command -- or rather, personally to the commander of the Pristina Corps. It has to do with the implementation of the education and training programme and combat training of Combat Group 1. The report is being submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Briefly, the first paragraph pertains to the 14th, the 14th of January. I would like to ask you to explain what this document says and what it pertains to, starting from the fourth paragraph; that is to say, from the words "On the 15th of January, 1999."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 15th of January, 1999, units from the Dulje sector carried out regular tactical training, T-9 training, 'a mechanised platoon on the march' along trig 915, Ljubovce village; trig 988, Garamele; 1160, Rance village; 1027 axis, and back." That means that part of the unit, the strength that we mentioned yesterday, up to platoon strength, was carrying out a programme according to training -- combat training along this axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: During this training, was this a unit -- was this unit attacked?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here that during this training, there was an attack against the unit that was conducting the training. Fire was returned. Since the terrorist forces fled, the unit could not get any closer to the village of Rance. It was about a kilometre away because of the deep snow. The snow was about 1 metre deep. The unit returned after that without having sustained any losses. If necessary, I can read all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No need. Thank you. The document is there. The document is in front of us. Please, did anyone enter built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single built-up area was entered. I and the corps commander strictly forbade any entry into built-up areas, especially during training. Axes that were chosen for training were roads that are in the hilly mountainous areas, that is to say, where there is no population or where there is the least number of houses, villages, in order to prevent any disturbances among the civilian population, as we usually say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next paragraph. In actually fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Scroll down the document, please, in B/C/S; and English also, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the last paragraph and the one before that, do you actually describe what happened -- or let me be even more specific. From whom did you receive this information that you entered in the last two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This describes the information from the encirclement around my combat group. I received this information from the chief of the Urosevac SUP, who was in charge of this action. As for the data I entered here, it was information that I received from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, was your unit in that area, on the basis of an agreement, or due to other needs?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to give a wider explanation. In view of the agreement that was in force, one of the three combat groups that were in the area of Kosovo and Metohija was Combat Group 1, from my unit, that was at the Dulje pass at a military facility, which was supposed to be earlier on a command post of the Pristina Corps. So that's the area where the unit was. It was practically a military area. The unit was there from April onwards, and according to the agreement, it remained in that area; of course, diminished, in terms of the strength provided then. Namely, 150 men along with combat equipment. In order to protect one of the most endangered areas -- or rather, axes from Kosovo towards Metohija, that is to say, through the Crnoljevo gorge and the Dulje pass, it was requested in that period that a smaller part of that combat group remain in Canovica Brdo; that is to say, right above the municipal assembly of Stimlje, and the town of Stimlje itself. The task of this smaller group was primarily to defend themselves in that area and to keep rapid deployment forces there that can follow military columns that were coming in from Pristina and going towards Metohija and the other way around; that is to say, that they were used to secure these columns along those 20 or 25 kilometres via Crnoljevo gorge, the Dulje pass, all the way to Suva Reka. These vehicles that were there were primarily BRDMs and Pragas, so they can actually follow motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the OSCE mission visit these units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, immediately after the agreement. The mission of the OSCE and our commissions who worked with them toured all these combat groups, and there were several tours that took place. At first there were some smaller problems, until the strength was at agreed levels; that is to say, October, November. And from then the personnel levels did not go up or down. They were constant. These commissions very often visited both parts of this combat group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, was fire opened at these forces of yours?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in this period that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The terrorist action of the MUP started in the morning. I do not remember their exact plan, but it was around dawn, 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. They carried out a blockade. Their action started, if I remember correctly, around 7.00. So practically, that part was blocked by the MUP forces. Around 8.00 or 9.00 from the area of Belince - that is to say, 300 or 400 metres away - fire was opened from a Browning and from mortars at our area -- at our positions. On that basis -- or rather, as soon as fire was opened, the unit took up defence positions straight away. Of course, in accordance with a plan that had previously been set and trained, and returned fire to this plateau above Belince that had no name. After a few exchanges of gunfire primarily from the BRDM and Praga, after about an hour or an hour and a half, there was no more fire: I would like to note that even 82-millimetre mortars were used, which in this process their commander, I think -- in one of the trials, rather, their commander -- Bujo was his name, I think, he said that he did open fire at the military from that pinewood; that is to say, Canovica Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, what size was your platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The size of this unit was a reinforced company; meaning about 150 men. But in two places. And we can say conditionally that there was a third one there too, if we take into account the unit that was on the move all the time escorting columns from Stimlje to Suva Reka, meeting them in Suva Reka, and then taking them back too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question is simply about the group that -- that were fired upon. How big was that platoon? It's described in your report as a "mechanised platoon on the march."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] BRDMs and one Praga opened fire. Two combat vehicles. They were right by the road. And they were waiting for the military convoys and accompanying them. As they were waiting for the military column, since fire had been opened, they returned fire. And after that, all combat activities stopped vis-a-vis the military; whereas, the other units took up positions for circular defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that your whole company was actually on that road when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to give a small clarification. This was a pinewood that was about 300 to 400 metres to the north of those two combat vehicles, camouflaged in the woods. They had their positions. Whereas, these two pieces of equipment were by the road and they were meeting vehicles that came up, and these vehicles opened fire -- or rather, returned fire to the village of Belince -- or rather, a bit to the south-east of Belince, about 400 or 500 metres to the south-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Just to clarify not more about that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us just clarify this. Is that the smaller part of your combat group that was attacked in the Stimlje area?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the smaller part that was attacked in Canovica Brdo -- or after -- rather, the broader area of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was attacked exactly?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit that was securing -- or rather, meeting the column comes from Pristina in order to go via Crnoljevo and further on to Suva Reka. And all of that is very close by, three to four hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: Could Mr. Cepic please not speak at the same time as the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you'll need to start that question again. You're overlapping with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many are there in the crews serving those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 12 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many people came under the attack? Could you please just clarify that, General.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those 12 men came under the attack. Those people who were there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: Could Mr. Cepic please not speak at the same time as the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you're being asked yet again not to speak at the same time as the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My apologies to interpreters. My apologies to this Honourable Trial Chamber. I will slow down. Could we have page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, on page 2 of this document, is there a description of these events that you just described to us in the previous few minutes?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is more or less what I've just explained to you. That is the gist of it, the location of the units, the positions that they manned, and the sectors where they set up the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us move on to another topic now. This is the area of responsibility. And my question to you is whether you were responsible for the entire situation in the area of responsibility of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as the brigade commander, was responsible for the entire situation in the area of responsibility of my brigade in the combat disposition of the troops; in other words, sectors that had been manned by military units were under my full responsibility. I was responsible before my commanders and before the law. Everything else that was outside of the defence sector, this was the jurisdiction of the MUP, of the judicial organs, of the civilian authorities, all those elements that were in charge of providing safety and security for property and persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would we have in e-court system 5D658, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document from the command of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. The date is the 6th of April, 1999, and it has to do with the maintenance of the security regime as ordered. It's an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain paragraph 1 or item 1 in this order.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your areas of responsibility, in coordination with the forces of the Republic of Serbia MUP, implement the security regime in full with the focus on protecting the units, the wartime equipment -- or combat equipment, maintaining public order, and protecting the civilian population." What this means is the following: Our troops are responsible for the safety and security of their own units and for the safety of their equipment that they have. And as for the civilian population and the public order, this is the responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we please now look at item 4.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Item 4 reads: "Provide assistance to the MUP organs in the efforts to return and protect the displayed persons." It is quite natural. One always has to provide assistance to persons -- or rather, state authorities in the performance of their tasks. This is one of the aspects of coordination and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at item 5.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Take strict measures to hold responsible all persons who violate the security regime." What this means is that all those who violate the law have to be treated in accordance with the law. All measures under the law have to be taken against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, could you please tell us, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My immediate superior, the one who was authorised to issue orders to me and to my brigade, was the commander of the Pristina Corps, General Vladimir Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And who did you report to in your reports?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally, in line with the chain of command, I was responsible to and I could only report to him, and my brigade command, the organs of the brigade command, reported to the command of the Pristina Corps, depending on their actual department and the task that they had been given. So only the Pristina Corps Command or the Pristina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system Exhibit number 51972. Not 5D but P probably. It's my mistake. Yes. P1972, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, did you receive this document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received several such documents at the brigade command with this -- bearing this title, "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How did you receive such documents?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those documents, like all the other documents, were received mostly by post. Let me explain. Post was delivered several times a week -- it actually depended. If there were any combat action, it arrived very rarely. Then it came through liaison officers and couriers. It came to the brigade. Together with this document, there was the excerpt from the decision of the Pristina Corps commander regarding the execution of a task, and all the other accompanying documents. Usually it was engineers support, logistics support, intelligence support, and other forms of support that have to follow after a decision of a Pristina Corps commander to the brigade commands in order for this brigade to be able to carry out its task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was this document for you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basic document that I would receive was the -- an excerpt from the decision of the Pristina Corps commander. It was on a map for the execution of a task. And this is one of the documents that pertained to the coordination with the Ministry of Interior forces for the destruction of the forces in a certain area. In this case, we are talking about Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You mentioned "coordination." How did you implement this coordination?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coordination in the brigade and lower down was carried out through the SUP chief and his organs in the relevant sectors or departments. Those were people that he appointed. The coordination was carried out through face-to-face contact. An agreement was reached to carry out joint tasks. So there was a very strict division of labour, and the way in which the Minister of Interior forces were supported was also clearly defined. Usually radio equipment would be exchanged and one or two officers would be exchanged in order to be able to coordinate the specific task, the execution of that specific task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And who did you meet from the MUP ranks in a specific situation?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally would meet with the Urosevac SUP chief, Bogoljub Janicijevic. And he was the only person that I coordinated those tasks with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, the Prosecution often alleges that there was a Joint Command in the sense of the command. As far as you were concerned, did a Joint Command exist in the sense of a command?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, only one command existed in the vertical chain of command; that was the Pristina Corps Command. And in the depth, I was the commander. I was the command for the subordinate units. So no joint commands existed for me, because I carried out all the orders that I received from the Pristina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 5.3, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, you're going to go on to other parts of this document, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Count 5.3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, do you see on the screen in front of you item 5.3?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Does this pertain to your unit, setting up the blockade along the Canovica Brdo-Crneljevo-Dulje pass axis?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this pertains to my brigade, which is tasked with setting up a blockade along this line that you just defined: Canovica Brdo, Crnoljevo, and Dulje pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, on the basis of this document, did you draft your own order?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Every document that came from the Pristina Corps Command - it is an order - has to be implemented all the way down to the lowest level. In order to be able to do so, the brigade command -- or rather, I have to write my own order for the implementation of the order that was received from the Pristina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see the first page, please, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the date on this document, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us just zoom in a bit. Okay, that's fine. This is the 14th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we leave --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we leave this one, can I see the last page, please. Mr. Jelic, you'll see that this document is not signed or stamped -- well, sorry, it -- it's not signed or stamped at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you recognise the stamp in the top right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can hardly read it. It's not very legible. I can just read two letters, J and E, and I can't see anything else. Perhaps you might assist in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a stamp that was on it when you received it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that, because I can't recognise this stamp. I'm not sure whether that is the stamp that was on it or whether it was on it at all, because I simply cannot read anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you received orders from your superiors, did they normally have either a signature or a stamp or perhaps both on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, documents bear both. We received documents at the brigade in a single envelope, sealed, and they bore the stamps of the Pristina Corps Command. They were received at the brigade command. They were entered in the registry, the logbook. And then the mail was opened and inspected. So the correspondence -- the documents were then inspected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So is this one unusual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This document is unusual, if you compare it with the classical combat orders. But for us it pertained to the coordination, what to do together with the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other Joint Command documents that you received, were they signed or stamped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did receive some documents from -- that were entitled "The Joint Command." They were more or less like this one. I don't recall that any of them were actually signed. I can't remember. But the format was more or less the same as this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did I rightly understand you to say that with this document there would also be an extract from the Pristina Corps order and that extract would be the part of the order that applied to your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That mail, there would also be the excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's just clarify for Their Honours. What precisely was in that mail? What did you receive specifically in that envelope from the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that in that envelope, apart from this document, there would be an extract on a map from the decision of the commander of the Pristina Corps specifically for my brigade. Furthermore, the plan of contact and coordinated action with all -- and communications with all the units participating, engineering, and rear support, intelligence and other forms of support, and all these documents would be signed by the commander of the Pristina Corps. They would be registered in the Pristina Corps Command and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw from the document on the screen, item 5 -- 5.3, and we saw that a blockade is requested on the axis mentioned. Could we now look at 5D369, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, document is 5D1369, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to object to the use of this document. It's only been partially translated. As you can see, it's a two-page document, and we have one line that has been translated in English, at least that's what we have been provided. And I don't think it really assists the Chamber to have an incomplete translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, what do you say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for well-known reasons, because time is so short, we asked only for the most important sentence, in our view, to be translated, and we will be very, very happy to have the entire document and it's in our interest to have the entire document translated as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- what has been your plan? Is it to simply have one line -- one passage translated, or the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To ask for a translation of the whole document. I have to mention that we had very little time to have translations done of all the documents. Our learned friend Mr. Hannis objected and said we had over 40 untranslated documents relating to witness Jelic. That was three days ago, if I recall correctly. And today, due to the expeditiousness of the translation service, we have reduced this to a very small number of documents, only two or three. It is our plan and our wish to have entire document -- the entire documents translated, all these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand your submission about having very little time to have it translated. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document arrived on a later list, in an additional request. We asked for it to be included last week. It is untranslated and it was not used in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But why -- why did you wait until last week?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our investigators did not find everything we requested right away. This document was admitted by a decision of the Trial Chamber, and the Prosecution did not object to the document itself but only to the photograph of the heads of members of the Army of Yugoslavia, which have been cut off, when we asked for this document to be admitted. And they agreed to having this document included in our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that -- that would be on the assumption that it would be translated when it came into court, presumably. That's -- the problem is not they accept it being added to the 65 ter list; the problem is the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. I mean, our position -- we do not -- we do not oppose to -- the addition of this document to the 65 ter list. It's just the use of one line of the document. And I would like to point out that it's not the only document that the Defence intends to use with this witness that's only been partially translated. There's a second document, it's 5D789, and there's also only one paragraph translated from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One possible solution, of course, is for us to admit only the part of the document that's been translated. Does that cause a difficulty for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I believe it does, Your Honour. I think the document needs to be read in its entirety by the Chamber in order to appreciate the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, we're not satisfied that appropriate steps have been taken to have documents translated in time for the presentation of your Defence case, and we are going to refuse to allow this document to be used at all. And this may have ongoing repercussions in the presentation of your Defence case, but hopefully it will bring home to you the importance of getting these documents properly prioritized and translated. We are not going to bounce back and forward in the presentation of Defence cases because documents have not been adequately dealt with in preparation. So move to something else, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I will move on, but based on the instructions we received earlier in relation to untranslated documents, I understood our instructions to be that only a certain part of the text was to be translated, but we will ask for this entire document to be translated probably today and we'll ask to admit it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, let's be clear about this. You consider the whole of this document to be necessary. It needs therefore to be considered in its context, which is through the witness we now have before us. You're absolutely right. If it's not necessary to have the whole of a document, you only need to translate the part that is necessary. So please don't confuse the two issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the needs of the presentation of my Defence case, the paragraph on the monitor is quite sufficient. The Prosecution objected, saying they needed the entire text. I don't need it. The sentence on the screen is sufficient for me. But in order to avoid the Prosecution having any doubts about the document, I agree to the entire document being translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you made it clear your intention was to have the document translated in its entirety. You accept their position on this that the whole of it is necessary to understand the position. We've made our decision. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm afraid I may have been misunderstood, but, of course, in compliance with Your Honour's decision, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, based on the previous document I showed you, did you issue your own orders?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every document received from the Pristina Corps Command, especially if it relates to the execution of a combat task, the unit commander - in this case, me - is duty-bound to receive the document, to inform the corps commander personally that he has received the order for an action, or for the execution of a combat task; and when the task is received, after this little check, the task is studied and the commander issues his own decision based on the corps commander's decision for the execution of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Based on this document, did you issue your decision in that specific situation?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I issued my own order for the execution of the task which was in the coordination and which was contained in the corps commander's decision on the map and all the accompanying documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, this document which has not been allowed is the very document representing his own order based on the previous document, and it was only my intention to demonstrate the continuity by date and by task to show that one document follows from another, which represents the brigade order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the sake of the record, the situation is the following: With this refusal to admit this document, Sainovic's Defence has also been damaged, because this document demonstrate that there is no Joint Command being reported to, and that's why the Prosecution is objecting. I myself will ask for this document to be translated and to be admitted at a later date, because our own client is also having his case damaged because of the failure to admit this document. Let me remind you that the Prosecution also would read just little bits of documents which had not been translated in their entirety. Mr. Hannis did that on at least 20 occasions. And for the sake of the truth, none of us objected. But let us then have the possibility of the general reading out what it says, because this really is to the detriment of my client, and I hope you -- Your Honours will understand this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will not revisit this matter. The matter has been dealt with. You didn't raise your position at that time. Your Defence is not being presented by Mr. Cepic. It's your job to present your defence. That stage is past. There are occasional opportunities when cross-examination by coincidence will give you an opportunity to raise other matters. In this instance, the document will not be admitted through this witness. Let's proceed. Carry on, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For the sake of the record, my client is being prejudiced even more with a non-admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will not tolerate defiance in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have in e-court system Exhibit Number 5D1285, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, is this a document issued by you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's from my brigade, dated the 19th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What does this document represent?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a regular daily combat report sent to the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What are you reporting about to the Pristina Corps Command in this document which is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, firstly, about the enemy, the forces of the enemy. And that's according to the regular procedure as to the format of telegrams sent to the command. Will you let me read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just briefly. One sentence only. In item 2.1, the second sentence -- or rather, the second paragraph, beginning with the words "according to the decision."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. "According to the decision of the 17th of April, 1999, parts of the brigade are engaged in blocking and scattering the Siptar terrorist forces. This action is still in progress." And that's the next document sent to the corps command in the realization of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This reporting, does it have to do with the order you issued that was mentioned previously and the document headed "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document linked to both of these documents. In fact, it's a report being sent based on the order issued by the Pristina Corps commander. He issued the task, and I am now reporting back to him concerning the situation and what the units are doing at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on. General, did you ever report to some sort of Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Not a single report of mine coming from the brigade was ever sent to any other command except the Pristina Corps Command or the Pristina Corps commander personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 5D683, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the document we see on the screen, is it issued by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's from the command of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade -- or Motorised Brigade, dated the 15th of May, 1999, and addressed to the Corps Pristina Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 2.1, beginning with the words: "In the area of the village of Raka."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very clearly legible here, but I can see it. "In the sector of the village of Raka, numerous documents of the Siptar terrorist forces were found with specific information about the activities of the Siptar terrorist forces, the Army of Yugoslavia, and the MUP. These documents show the connection of the OSCE forces with the NATO forces, for whom they have been collecting intelligence."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We have the text. You don't have to read it out. Do you happen to recall, as we do have the text before us, whether this material, this information you found, was correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information we found in the village of Raka and its area corresponded fully with the organisational and establishment structure of the brigade, especially heavy combat weapons. There was a list of all the weapons we had with PVO tables, Browning, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date? I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Please scroll up.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 15th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, did you have any volunteers in your unit?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had volunteers in my unit from the end of March until the beginning of April, in that period. That's when most of the volunteers reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What kind of status did they acquire by arriving the unit?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Law on Armed Forces, the law on the army, a volunteer is only a person in respect of the way in which he reports to a unit in the Army of Yugoslavia. These are usually persons who do not have a wartime assignment or who were not engaged anywhere. As they arrive in the Army of Yugoslavia, they are no longer termed "volunteers." They are practically soldiers, members of the military group that they are in. There is no difference, therefore, between them and regular soldiers, not in terms of their rights or responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, how were they admitted, taken in, and how were they deployed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Volunteers were taken in in an organised manner, as far as I know, in the 1st Army and in our army. Now, in talking about our army, it took place in Nis. Then they were selected -- or rather, checked. There were checkups of the state of their health and their psychological and physical abilities. Then also at the training grounds of Medja, they were trained. And after this training, at the level of the army command, they joined units. And once they would arrive in a unit, they were assigned to units in accordance with the VES, the military evidentiary specialty, that they had while they served their term in the military before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You have extensive military experience. Did you have any duties in a special unit?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was commander of a sabotage unit in the detachment of the army, and also I was head of a military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In view of your overall military training and experience and the positions of military doctrine and military science, what is the ratio of forces needed in order to neutralise a terrorist group?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our standards that are appropriate to what prevailed at the end of the last century, this meets European and world standards. Between 15 and 20. That is what the ratio should be. That is to say, 15 to 20 to 1; that is to say, seven or eight times more than in carrying out an ordinary combat task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In this courtroom, we often heard the concept of excessive use of military force. Can you tell us whether in our combat rules there is any reference to that.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our combat rules and the literature that I studied, we do not come across this term of "excessive use of force" as a military term. This is more of an analytical matter, when one analyses certain events, when one analyses the situation, the ratio of resources used vis-a-vis the objective attained. So it depends on whether it is attack or defence, what kind of action is concerned. It is customary to say "excessive use of force" by way of jargon; that is to say, that inadequate resources were used for attaining a certain objective. However, if we see the standards there used in the fight against this evil of terrorism at the end of the last century, especially in this beginning of this century, combat against terrorism practically requires a fight with all available resources used in order to destroy it. So there is no ratio that can say whether it is a cannon, a rifle, a Praga, whatever. If we see what the International Community is doing nowadays for this kind of fight, even the Air Force and helicopters are used too, which is only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, I'm interested in what kind of use was there of combat resources during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period of the war, we had several orders, and that is what we also did on our own. We used our resources in the most rational possible way only if our combat resources were directly attacked. The reason for this was that there was absolute supremacy on the side of NATO in air. Therefore, our combat equipment, especially heavy combat equipment, would have been detected and therefore destroyed. So we used it in a highly rational manner and ultimately we were preparing for defence in case of a land invasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you tell me, how much ammunition was spent during the wartime period?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can best be seen from our reports. If you have them, practically you can add up the ammunition used during those three months. But it was about .3 to .5 -- or rather, 3 to 5 per cent of the combat kits of military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit number 5D670, please. [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the mentioned document, we do not have a translation. That is what my assistant has just told me. Can we produce the document in the following way: I will ask the witness to read out a certain part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your position on this document, Ms. Kravetz?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have already stated our position, or at least Mr. Hannis has, regarding untranslated documents. It has been very difficult for us to prepare for cross-examination of these witnesses because a lot of the documents have been translated late and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But we would like to know whether you're objecting to the admission of this document. We can only deal with them as and when they arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For this document, I propose that what we can do is that the witness reads out the passage that Mr. Cepic wants to rely on and that it be submitted for translation later. And so marked for identification at this stage and admitted when we get a full translation. I'm -- I maintain the position that I think for the Chamber to be able to properly assess these documents, a full English translation is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can't lose sight of the fact that these are essentially adversarial proceedings and it's important when we don't know exactly what's coming but the parties are more aware of the evidence that's coming and to be anticipated that there's consistency in the position taken. Now, it may be that it will become clearer as we encounter any further problems with translation that there is a consistency in the position taken, but we encourage the parties to take a consistent line. We see that what's being said by the Prosecution here is itself consistent with what happened during the presentation of the Prosecution case, that there were occasions when documents were translated so far as necessary in court and marked for identification. There's no objection to that course of action here, so we will allow you to deal with the document that way, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For the sake of clarity, Mr. Hannis and I had practically daily communication in relation to untranslated documents. I sent him an e-mail with documents that had not been translated at that point in time, and I gave him timely information on our problems with translation; and I communicated to him daily on the redaction of that particular number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I need to respond to that. We have a number of communications about that. But one of the points that I've raised concern about regards the upcoming witnesses after this one, we still have untranslated documents for Mr. Filipovic and several for General Delic. Now, I've been told that the number of documents that Mr. Cepic intends to use has been reduced, but I don't know which ones he is not going to use, because I haven't seen the notification for next week. I've been told it has been filed, but I've been told basically it's the same list as was last week. So I still don't know which ones he's not going to use, and that doesn't help me prepare, so I -- I would request assistance on that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's concentrate in the courtroom on the presentation of evidence, and you can continue your discussions on these matters during the breaks. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document from the command of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade dated the 22nd of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What does this document represent? Could you please read to me the heading of the document and the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Execution of combat activities in the areas of deployment. Order. Issued to." "On the basis of the order of the command of the Pristina Corps, strictly confidential number 455-247, dated the 21st of March [as interpreted], 1999, and with a view to destroying and crushing leftover Siptar terrorist forces in the regions of the disposition of units, I hereby order."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] A little bit scrolled down, please. Count 7 I need.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: We misspoke. It is not March. It's May.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please read item 7.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Movement of combat equipment in the sectors of deployment are not to be carried out, because there is a risk of NATO air-strikes."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at item 3, the second sentence therein, "I prohibit."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. "I prohibit the relocation of units outside of their assigned sector of deployment without prior approval of the superior command."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why is this order important?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the NATO Air Force had air superiority. The terrorist forces were constantly attacking the positions. And if those units were to move out of their positions, they would have been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you sustain any losses in the unit just before the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as on the eve of the war, during the war, we sustained constant attacks in our unit up until the very end of the war, and we sustained substantial casualties. I'm now referring to personnel, the troops. A total of 24 soldiers were killed in the brigade, soldiers and officers, and 88 were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether the terrorist attacks were at the same level of intensity until your unit withdrew from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the very moment when the Kumanova Agreement was signed, our units were constantly under particular attack, and particularly that was in the case in the last few days, as the Kumanova Agreement was being negotiated or drafted and signed. Particularly on the axes Urosevac, Kacanik, Djeneral Jankovic, Urosevac, Globocica, and in the area of the border with the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system 5D679, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, does this document corroborate what you just told us about the casualties sustained at the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the documents that confirms that, and it says here that 2nd Lieutenant Dragan Beko was killed in this area and two soldiers were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was the axis or road when they were killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the road leading to Stimlje -- or rather, to Doganovic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system 5D680, please. Do we have this document in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, does this document confirm the same thing?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my document. That confirm it is same thing. The date is the 6th of June, 1999. It was an entering combat report sent to the Pristina Corps Command. And it says here that Captain Milenkovic -- Milan Milenkovic was killed in the Kacanik area on the Djeneral Jankovic-Urosevac road. It was an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, how were the arrested persons treated?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war, we arrested people -- we arrested civilians only if they were in the border belt or if they were in the area of the combat deployment of the units, and the military police units would do so if some crimes were committed. All persons who were placed under the arrest were then processed. They were questioned by the security organs and the military police in the unit, and then they were sent on. They would either be tried or whatever. But they were always treated extremely humanely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a document, 5D678, it has not been translated. It speaks about this issue. Can we please show this document to the witness in the same manner as we have done so in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your position on this, Ms. Kravetz?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We can proceed in that same manner as with the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at item 1.1, the second paragraph therein. First of all, what is this? What is this document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my document that was sent as a regular combat report to the Pristina Corps Command, and it is not very legible, but let me try and read it, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Fine. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At around 4.15 hours in the Kodra Fura sector, the Kodric border post, four persons attempted to cross the state border illegally from the Republic of Macedonia. When they were stopped, they opened fire. Fire was returned and two of those persons who had tried to illegally cross the border were wounded. One of them was captured and the others fled to the territory of the Republic of Macedonia. The captured person will be handed over to the security organs at 11.20 hours in the Sahas Cesma sector" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's quite sufficient. Does this document confirm what you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely what I've just told you about the treatment of the unknown persons and civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, where were they kept in custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every person in cases of this kind, who was arrested, was immediately handed over to the security organ. They exist at a level of the artillery battalion and battalion. That organ carries out the preliminary interview, and based on that decides who to hand over this person, whether to military prosecutor's office or to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And where would they be held in custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly in the building where the unit was, or in the facility where the unit was. If it was a border belt, as was this case, they were held where the command of that unit was, at the border post. But one of the border -- there were border posts all over the place, but one of the border posts was always designated as the command of that particular border battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you were regarding these people as criminals, rather than prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those persons were criminals, to all intents and purposes. They violated the laws of the state by crossing into the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And if -- those who were moving in the areas of the deployment of the units, they were not prisoners of war; they had violated the -- some provisions in the law and they were treated accordingly. These could not be prisoners of war. They were our citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just one brief question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the higher-level units, were there specific buildings designated as detention units for people of that kind?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the brigade level, there was no such institution or no such building. Wherever -- but in all units, there were security organs, and they dealt with those people immediately after their arrest. That had nothing to do with the brigade command. The brigade command or the commands of the units had nothing much to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, the units of your brigade during the war, and throughout the armed conflict in Kosovo and Metohija, did they apply the rules of international humanitarian law and laws and customs of war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the rules of the international humanitarian law were complied very strictly in accordance with the law. Dozens of orders that had been received from the military top and down from the corps command, and they were disseminated to lower-ranking units and all the way down to the soldiers, and this also was the case with the rules of combat. We all had to comply with those provisions of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did every soldier in your unit have instructions for the conduct in combat?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade command received relevant instructions, and every soldier had a laminated pocket-sized brochure instructing him how to comport himself in the war, with all the relevant obligations those soldiers had to abide by, and every soldier in the brigade received that. He was issued with that. And I am also referring now to the professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 4 please. 5D1284, please. I need in B/C/S page 7; in English, page 10, please. Please scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look at the last-but-one item on the page that you have in front of you on the screen. If you can please read it.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. As you can see, this is an order that I issued. And it says here: "In all situations, consistently observe the provisions of international law of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the rules that you are bound by, the rules of service and other documents, do they also stipulate the application of the international law of war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is defined both in the rules of service and in the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This was the law. We had to comply by that. We had to abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we see Exhibit number P1306, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, did you receive this order that you can see in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise it. I can't see very clearly what it says here, because I -- I have to look at the bottom of the document. But based on the contents, I can say that I received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 662, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your order?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my order from the brigade command. The date is the 17th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What does this order pertain to, the one that we can see in front of us on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order pertains to the protection of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was the basis for this order of yours?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I issued this order on the basis of the order from the -- from the corps command, and because of the coordinated action by the NATO air-strikes and terrorists, the measures that were envisaged here had to be taken. But I have to say that my copy is hardly legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in the B/C/S version to enable the witness to see it more clearly. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, could you please explain to us: In accordance with the law in force in our country, whose responsibility was it to protect the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian authorities had to protect the civilians. The community that was functioning throughout the war, the municipal authorities and all the other organs that existed at a municipal level. This was not something that the combat units were supposed to do, because their purpose was completely different. Furthermore, the Minister of the Interior forces provide support to them in this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 5D665, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the document comes up on the screen, General, could you clarify something in the transcript that isn't quite clear, so I'll ask you again. Whose duty was it to look after the civilians, please?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the civilian structures, the state structures on the territory, and the MUP forces that had this duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: To whom did the MUP provide assistance?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the municipal assemblies, the judiciary, the judicial organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel and witness not overlap, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in B/C/S also this document, 5D665, please. This is the wrong document on our screens. This is the previous document, so we need that. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I saw in English, but not in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, that, according to the e-court system, is 5D665.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, in English, but not in B/C/S. We haven't got the same document. I have in hard copy and you have in electronic version in English, so with your leave, we can pass this copy to the witness, please. Yes, now we have in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's important that you check the e-court entry and rectify it if there is a difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My assistant already checked, and it appears in B/C/S. And as I said previously, I saw in English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, you can proceed with the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Could we have back in English on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have the English on the screen, page 2 though.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We need the first page, just -- I'm afraid that it is not the same document. 5D665. It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your problem now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We will solve the situation during the break, so I can move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we can have the break just now, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, we have to break at this stage. That will be for half an hour or so. While we have the break, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We solved the situation and -- actually the problem, and we have on our screens right now Exhibit 5D665. We have a problem with the English. We have the document in B/C/S but not in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Perfect. And could we have also in B/C/S, please. Again a problem. The same problem. The right side of the screen is correct, but on left-hand side -- we need in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now in B/C/S. Excellent. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the General, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document from my brigade, the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. It's dated the 23rd of April, 1999. It's an order on the protection of the civilian population in the brigade zone's -- zone -- brigade zone of responsibility where combat is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Combat operations zone. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just very briefly, what is the purpose of this order?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this order is that all units subordinate to me at battalion level should act humanely, look after the civilian population, avoid losses of casualties among civilians in their areas of responsibility in their defence zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, did displaced persons return to their homes during the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Displaced persons returned to their homes on the eve of the aggression and also in the course of the aggression. They returned to their villages, their homes, the places from which they had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Exhibit number 5D1286, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this a document from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document from my brigade, dated the 16th of April, 1999. Addressed to the command of the Pristina Corps, and it's urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you please read the part that begins in item 1.1, the second passage, it begins with the words "on the 16th of April or since" --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 16th of April, at 0800 hour, above the village of Kisela Voda leaflets were ejected. A large number of refugees is using trains, buses, and tractors to come back from the Republic of Macedonia and they are returning in the direction of Kacanik. On the same day, the 16th of April, 1999, from 1410 to 1450 hours, NATO aviation struck in the sector of Glavica, Varos Selo, and Nekodim. Eight missiles were fired on the sector of deployment of the mixed anti-tank artillery battalion" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we can see that. We have the text before us. Would you please explain to us this fire which is described here and these military activities, were they close to the road where the refugees were -- on which the refugees were moving?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main road leading from Kosovo-Metohija to Macedonia and vice versa is a main road, and there is also a railway next to it. Here one can see that the civilians are returning to their villages, which are listed here, and the Air Force -- the aircraft is firing on their villages precisely at the time when they are returning to them. There are several villages enumerated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the course of NATO air-strikes, did NATO use in the areas of Kacanik and Urosevac cluster bombs and depleted uranium to fire on civilian and military targets?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more than once the NATO aircraft dropped cluster bombs, both on the positions and the areas and villages to the south and north of Urosevac and also on the town of Urosevac itself. And that's not counting the barracks, which they fired on incessantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 5D660, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, does this document confirm what you said?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a document issued by me, sent to the Pristina Corps Command, confirming what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On this list of targets fired on, are there civilian facilities?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, besides the military facilities listed here, such as barracks, we have firing on villages, such as the villages of Palic, Grebno, Pitina [phoen], the factory in Doganovici, the village of Banjica. And these are all civilians target which were hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is this a document issued by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the original document I sent to the Pristina Corps Command as information on the events of the day. This comes from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Here we see in one of the sentences that atomic biological technical recognize has shown that there was no radiation in these sectors.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever NATO air-strikes were conducted, there was atomic biological chemical reconnaissance conducted. We had a team constantly reconnoitering the whole area wherever NATO projectiles hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you have expert teams for clearing up the terrain which carried out this job?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a team for the clearing up of this terrain, primarily to remove, destroy, and mark these places. That was a team at corps level, which was organised, and we sent telegrams to report to the corps command about this. The team was from the RV, which had been attached to the corps, and it serviced all the units on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. It was not part of the brigade but, rather, part of the corps. It was an expert -- and the experts came from the RV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, what was done at the Silkapor factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Silkapor factory was a civilian facility. It was targeted at the time. There was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was it used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Silkapor factory, in the initial period of the war, there was a command post next to it. Immediately after the aggression, we had information that the NATO forces knew about us. They had information that the brigade command was in Doganovici, so we assumed it would be hit. Immediately after the aggression started, the command moved the command post from there, so that we did not have units in the building at that time. Five children, minors, 10 or 12 years old, were hit in that air-strike. They were all members of one family and they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The Silkapor factory, my question is not what was next to it but what did the factory manufacture?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Silkapor factory manufactured building construction material. These were blocks, 60 by 30 centimetres in size. This material was used to build buildings. It was similar to a brickworks, but it was a different kind of material, also used for masonry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And one further clarification. Twice you mentioned in your reply to my previous question "RV." What does "RV" mean?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "RV" means Air Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we have in e-court system 5D675, please. Unfortunately, we haven't got translation for this document. Again, the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest we proceed in the same manner as before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, please look at item 2.1. First I'll ask you to identify this document. What does it say in the heading?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my document from the 243rd Mechanised Brigade dated the 4th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
