utterances.text: Thank you. Item 2.1, the second paragraph begins with the word: "In the course of the 3rd of May, 1999." Could you read this, please.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the course of the 3rd of May, 1999, measurements of radioactive contamination were made on several locations in the general area of Dulje at trig point 925, a value was measured of 0.20 milliroentgen. In the area of trig point 868, a value of 0.26 milliroentgens was measured. And in the area of Ras Mahala [phoen], a value of 0.13 to 0.26 milliroentgen was measured. As the upper limit permitted of natural phones is up to 0.20 milliroentgens, there is evidently stronger radiation in individual locations targeted by NATO air-strikes."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, what measures did you take when you came across a situation like this one?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned just a little while ago, when one came across a place that had been struck, first the place had to be marked. The location had to be marked. Then the closest units, army units, had to be informed. And the civilians also had to be informed. If possible, on the very same day or a few days later, according to the plan of the team receiving this report in the corps command, the area would be sanitised or the offending material destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, on the 24th of March, 1999, what is the significance of that date for you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a characteristic day. It was the day when the aggression on the FRY by NATO started -- or rather, the NATO campaign started on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When did you leave the barracks and take up the defence areas?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All units from my brigade, all these units went out before the 24th of March. On that day, all the units had already taken up the defence areas to defend the country from aggression. The war and material reserves, according to plan, had already been taken out and stored in the depth of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 5D317, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what does this document represent?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a little bit? Can the contrast be sharpened? Because I can't see it very well. This is a document issued by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the intelligence administration, strictly confidential number 2-80, dated the 24th of March, 1999. It's information on NATO forces in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now please look at the paragraphs. What do they describe?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These paragraphs describe the strength of the forces and their country of origin. So it says: "From the 4th armoured Brigade, 1st Armoured Brigade, Great Britain; 21st Armoured Brigade, from the 7th Armoured Division, Germany; from the 2nd" -- I can't see this very well -- "France."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does this last sentence say? In English, it's on page 2.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "On the tanks, armoured personnel carriers, and self-propelled vehicles, there is visible written in white," and in quotation marks, "KFOR." [Realtime transcript read in error "K4"]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Not K4 but -- yes, exactly. Yes. Could we go to the second page in B/C/S, the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see the number of men and equipment that were in Macedonia at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see here that in the Republic of Macedonia there are about 12.500 soldiers, 100 tanks, 250 armoured personnel carriers, 52 artillery pieces, 36 helicopters, and 1.240 motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, these forces in Macedonia, how far were they in terms of kilometres from our state border and your units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These forces were about 20 to 30 kilometres away from the state border in depth into the territory, that is, a march of about 1 and a half hours with combat vehicles to the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, now we are going to move on to the other side of the border and we are going to go on dealing with the same date. The village of Kotlina, to the best of my knowledge, was it a terrorist stronghold?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Kotlina and the surrounding area, Ivaja, Pustanik, that's it. Those hamlets, constituted a very strong terrorist stronghold. There were several hundred terrorists [Realtime transcript read in error "International Red Cross"] in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The indictment in paragraph 72(k).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Somehow or other the International Red Cross has crept in, but it was simply terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. A completely different translation. I can ask again the same question or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, it's a question of court reporting transcribing, not of interpretation. The tape is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, just for the transcript, the village of Kotlina, was it a terrorist stronghold?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exceptionally strong of the terrorist forces in the part that has to do with the border belt, practically 5 or 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I'm going to put a few questions to you pertaining to the crime base in relation to these locations. Will it be easier for you if you have the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If possible. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1337.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, paragraphs in the indictment that have to do with the village of Kotlina are 72(k) and 75(k)(i). A Prosecution witness testified before the Trial Chamber, Hazbi Loku, and the indictment says in the briefest possible terms that "On or around the 8th of March, as regards the village of Kotlina, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked and partially burned, and then on the 24th of March, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia yet again attacked Kotlina with heavy weaponry and with the engagement of troops." Many men, residents of Kotlina, fled to the nearby woods during that attack and -- well, the forces of the FRY and Serbia ordered the women and children and elderly to board trucks which took them towards the town of Kacanik. Those who could not fit into the trucks were compelled to walk behind them towards Kacanik. A number of male residents of Kotlina were killed during this attack, including at least 17 men, whose bodies were thrown into wells. Before departing Kotlina, forces of the FRY and Serbia burned the remainder of the village. Many of the survivors fled to Macedonia." General, are these allegations correct, what I read out to you just now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Mr. Cepic, we have to have a foundation. We have to go through individual item, if that's what you -- you want to ask, but you can't ask a blanket question like that in relation to a whole of the section of the indictment. The answer would be valueless.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us deal with it in the right order in terms of the calendar. The 8th of March, 1999, General, it says that the village of Kotlina was attacked on or about the 8th of March. That is what Hazbi Loku, a witness here says. He says that the village was partly burned. And he says that the village of Ivaja was attacked on the same day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. The army never attacked a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- do you have any knowledge about the village of Ivaja in that period? Were there any actions in that area?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the mentioned period, in the period that you are talking about, in your question, according to the information that we received later, in that area there was an anti-terrorist action of the MUP forces; namely, a patrol of MUP forces was attacked there and the leader of that patrol, a captain, got killed. I think his name was Staletovic or something like that. And then the MUP forces searched the area looking for terrorists. Then a clash took place with the terrorist forces, and I know that the fight happened in that period. That is, the period between the 28th of February and the 8th or 9th of March. So that is the period concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us now move on to the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you -- before you do that, was that action confined to Ivaja or did it include the village of Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, this was an action vis-a-vis Kotlina. I cannot tell you exactly what the scope of this action was, because we did not participate. Through the exchange of information between the MUP and ourselves, I am aware of this information and that is the information we had made available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can we have the map on the screens, please. I would like to ask the general to indicate the village of Kotlina and the village of Ivaja to us and where the forces of the Army of Yugoslavia were in the area of defence disposition.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see it very well here. I am sorry. But roughly it is in this area. Kotlina and Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on our screens, so ... [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we use ELMO? Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a hard copy of the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you can use the ELMO, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that -- that screen is blank also. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please move it a bit, General. To the left, if possible. That's right. Just a bit more, please. Right. Now could you indicate the villages of Kotlina and Ivaja to us.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where the villages are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. Where were your forces, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My closest forces were at the in-depth security, here; that is, Combat Group 3 and Combat Group 21. These forces were about a kilometre and a half away from these villages. But they had been there for several months already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In order to lay a better foundation for this, what you've told us, I'm just going to ask you to use the marker and to put a circle around Kotlina, Ivaja, and your forces.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is that circle?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kotlina and Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you put number "1" there, please.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: To the left and on the other side where your forces are, could you please put a circle there and could you put numbers there as well.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] These are the positions. I'll go across this. These are the positions of the combat groups practically. Combat Group 3 and Combat Group 21, respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your opinion, why were these units in these positions that you marked?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, these units were preventing a spillover of forces from the Republic of Macedonia to the Republic of Serbia and vice versa, but now, at the same time, they were used for defending the country from a possible land invasion by NATO along these directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. On the 24th of March, 1999, did the army enter the mentioned villages, as Prosecution witness Hazbi Loku claimed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army never entered these villages. And I've already said that on the-- that the 24th of March was the most critical day for, generally speaking, for the Army of Yugoslavia, for the Pristina Corps for my brigade, and for every last soldier, because that was the time when all the units left barracks, took up defence positions, camouflaged them, tied up a firing system. That is a job that takes several days, to reach the third, fourth, or fifth level of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness claims that on that day, using heavy weaponry and troops, the villages of Kotlina and Ivaja were attacked. Did you attack these villages with artillery or in any other way?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these units that are at these positions are in the first level of defence. They were all fortified, and it was prohibited to use heavy weaponry. Furthermore, if heavy weaponry were to be used, that would constitute a demasking of their positions. Also, the roads there are very difficult to negotiate. If you take a careful look, you will see that the altitude is about 1.000 metres. There is still snow there. These are narrow village roads where practically combat vehicles cannot go. My previous order, before that, was to use that kind of weaponry only when the unit is directly attacked; that is to say, if the combat disposition of the unit is under immediate threat. So the unit did not open fire at the village and it had no reason to open fire at the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there any attacks against your units that were in the marked regions?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period, when the aggression started -- or rather, the air campaign, there was a very large-scale attack against all units that were there. The border battalion and the units that were involved in in-depth security. Golimo Brdo [phoen], Bijelo Brdo were attacked strongly from the area of Kotlina, vis-a-vis Combat Group 3. However, Combat Group 21 was attacked from the region of the village of Pustenik. So in that period, during those first ten days or so, very heavy fighting took place there with the terrorist forces. As soon as the area was taken up and as soon as any changes in combat deployment and equipment were prohibited, every unit had an intervention unit too; that is to say, for securing the area if there are forces that would be brought in during an incursion. So they would use smaller units. Basically, the unit -- the rapid deployment intervention unit took up the area of Bijelo Brdo to prevent terrorist attacks from these two hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, in repelling this attack, were heavy weapons used? Tanks, rather.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that tanks were not used in repelling this attack. For the most part, these were units that were equipped for rapid deployment, using reconnaissance vehicles, such as BRDMs and Pragas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the army participate in any way in destroying the mosques in Kotlina and Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the army did not enter these villages, and it did not destroy any religious or other buildings in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have quoted quite a few allegations made by Prosecution witness, Hazbi Loku. My final question: Are his allegations made vis-a-vis the army correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His allegations are not correct because indeed the army did not enter the village and it had no need to enter the village, because it was in the region; it could not carry out manoeuvres, movements of these units for the reasons I've already mentioned. This was a critical time for my brigade, as I've already said, and for the rest of the troops that were in the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just one more question in relation to Kotlina. The witness mentioned that military trucks were used for transporting civilians from Kotlina to Kacanik on the 24th of March. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for these truck, these vehicles, on that day, on that critical day, the army had them full of military equipment and ammunition, transport, logistics. This accompanies the combat disposition of units. We did not have motor vehicles for transportation and we did not have the capacities for that and we did not have trained men to be able to handle that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to move on to the town of Kacanik. That is 72(k)(ii) in the indictment. I am just going to tell you briefly what the indictment says, that "on or about the 27th and 28th of March, 1999, the forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the town of Kacanik, forces of the FRY and Serbia harassed, detained, beat, and shot" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, why do you need to read this? Why don't you ask questions about -- about -- about --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I will ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- about evidence and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I will do that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we had Isa Raka, a Prosecution witness who testified in this case, and he said that on March 27 and 28th of March 1999, the FRY and Serbian forces attacked the town of Kacanik. Did your forces attack the town of Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not attack the town of Kacanik. There was no reason to do so, there was no need to do so, because the municipal assembly and all the other organs, all the structures of the government functioned there, the MUP, the judiciary, and so on, there was no need for us to enter that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you have any combat positions in the town of Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no combat positions in the town of Kacanik. There were some to the north of the town -- or rather, to the north-west, but not in the town of Kacanik itself. And you can see that on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, can you remind me what that map is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an excerpt from the defence operation made by the Pristina Corps commander for my brigade. It was made immediately before the aggression started, on the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is its number, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For ID 1337, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And in the meantime, could we have the IC number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to be having anything else marked on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll wait until you've completed using it before we mark -- before we give it a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, Lami Sejdi, a Prosecution witness testified in this case, and he said that on the 13th of April, or about that date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you -- if you are -- if you're moving on, can I ask you, Mr. Jelic, do you know what other forces were around Kacanik on the 27th and 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On or around the 27th or 28th of March, in that period there were only the MUP forces in the town of Kacanik, given that this was the seat of the municipality and that the municipal assembly, the judiciary, the MUP, and all the other normal structures were operating there. Of course, the circumstances were difficult, because it was wartime, but they were functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did -- did you hear of -- of any anti-terrorist action around the 27th and 28th in Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 27th and the 28th - I can't recall the exact date - I know that there was an anti-terrorist action launched by the MUP forces. As far as I can recall, that was an attack from a rocket launcher or an Armbrust rocket launcher on a MUP patrol in the town of Kacanik itself, and a search was launched to locate those forces that ambushed those MUP forces. They wanted to find those terrorists, and I think that six or seven police officers were casualties in that attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you learn of the level of casualties of -- of the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that information, apart from what I've read. I don't have the data for that time, but by exchanging information with the SUP chief, because we exchanged information about terrorist forces whenever they appeared and attacked the MUP and -- or the military, but I don't know that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the hamlets of Slatina and Vata. We heard Lami Sejdi, a Prosecution witness in this case, and he claims that on the 13th of April or about that date the Serbian and FRY forces surrounded the village of Slatina and the hamlet of Vata. Did your forces surround those villages?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: Could the counsel please switch off his microphone. We hear a lot of background noise. It is very difficult to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not surround those villages. We did not enter those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: He goes on to say -- could you please indicate the village of Slatina and the hamlet of Vata on this map.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is on the road leading from Doganovic to Strbac. So this is the road to Strbac, this is the Prevalac pass. And further up that road, that leads to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, could you please circle this village and this hamlet on this map.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult to see that, but I will try to do so. This is in this area here. Yes. Slatina and Vata, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with a number.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We have 1, we have 2, we have 3 or -- rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The names are actually on the map, are they? The two -- the two names are there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, but it is very difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But that's good enough. We can identify it later with a magnifying glass, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: One of the main roads passes through that village, does it not?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of the main roads linking Kosovo with Metohija, through Strpce, and there is another part that leads to Macedonia to the Doganovic -- rather, the Ljuborcice [phoen] border post, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there any attacks launched on the vehicles moving on that road from that area?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very frequent attacks launched not from the villages but from areas outside of the villages. There were attacks on columns of vehicles that were bringing up logistics supplies to the units in the depth. That's Combat Group 3. So they were bringing in supplies to those units. The units that were actually bringing in supplies, they had their security detail. They could not just move about, just the drivers. But very often those columns would come under attack but not from the villages. It was always from the areas outside of the villages, usually on those hairpin bends and in the wooded areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, Witness Lami Sejdi in his evidence stated that a small plane had overflown the village and that the FRY and Serbian forces had used that plane to reconnoiter the area. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. The brigade does not have any aircraft. It didn't have any helicopters; it didn't have any aeroplanes. The corps command does not have any aircraft in its formation, in its establishment. It could be reinforced with such aircraft, but given the air supremacy of the -- of NATO, it would have been impossible to use any such aircraft. So we didn't have any of those. We didn't use any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The same Prosecution witness indicated that on the same date, the 13th, that on or about that day, the 13th of April, some forces entered the village and that they had red and black bandannas around their heads. Did members of your brigade wear any kind of bandannas or other kind of insignia? Could you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of my brigade, my units, wore only one kind of uniform, without any special insignia, bandannas or anything of the sort. There were no such units in the brigade, and I'm almost absolutely sure that there were no individuals who would be wearing things like that. So there were no special insignia apart from the standard ones that are defined in the rule -- rules of service and the rule on military attire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this village and around it, was there any KLA presence?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Siptar terrorist forces that were formed in brigades, one of those brigades existed in that area, to the south of Urosevac and all the way to Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did any people move out of that area before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- people did move out from this area before the war and during the war. Before the war, people mostly moved towards Urosevac. And during the war -- during the war, most of those people who emigrated went to the Republic of Macedonia. Although, some went to the Republic of Serbia, depending on the village from which they originated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about the villages of Slatina and Vata. Who carried out those movements in that area?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only the KLA, the terrorist forces, who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was the principle of two villages applied?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the reasons why people were moved out was to use this principle of two villages. One would be with -- inhabited -- and the other -- from the other one, people would move out. And then they would operate from one of those villages and then move back to protect themselves to the village where the civilian population lived, because those two villages were close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, were any anti-terrorist actions taken in this area in order to protect the roads?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no major anti-terrorist actions particularly on those roads leading to the -- to Macedonia, but there were some anti-terrorist actions in the direction towards Doganovici, Banjica, Old Banjica, and then further on to Strpce. There was an anti-terrorist action there because there was a risk that this road might be cut off, and for all intents and purposes that would have made it impossible for the civilians, MUP, and the army to move from Kosovo to Metohija and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In that action, what activities did the army take?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an action launched by the Ministry of the Interior and some elements from our unit provided support in those anti-terrorist actions. But that was close to the road leading to Strpce.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please show on the map - you don't have to make it if the names are there - the villages of Dubrava and Ruka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, before moving on, the date that we're concerned about in relation to Slatina is the 13th of April. And -- and an allegation of -- of a number of people being killed there. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This action was not carried out by the army. It was carried out by the Ministry of the Interior. And elements from my unit provided support to those units. We were not authorised to go into built-up areas or those buildings that were next to the road. This was in the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior, and at the same time they carried out the clear-up operations and investigations -- on-site investigation in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the same action that you were referring to taking place close to the road to Strpce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the action that took place on the road leading from Banjica to Strpce. But that was next to the road, in the road area. That was the only anti-terrorist action in that period. So then the army only provided support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did your exchange of information with the chief of the SUP advise your -- our explain to you whether the villages of Slatina and Vata had been entered by the MUP in -- as part of that anti-terrorist operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have information to the effect that they entered this village -- those villages, because I know -- as far as I know, they were restricted in their operations to the road area from the hairpin road that was there in the direction of Old Banjica because there were frequent attacks launched from there on civilian vehicles, military vehicles, and the MUP vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do you know nothing about the circumstances of the death of 13 civilians -- or 13 persons in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of that information in that period, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did you get information about any terrorists that had been killed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got some information indicating that -- indicating the number of terrorists who were killed on the basis of the number of pieces of weapons, but I can't now tell you how relevant that information was. I mean weapons that were seized in the course of this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please show us on this map the villages of Dubrava and Reka.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates] Well, these are the villages here and here, as far as I can see on this map; although, it's really a very small-scale map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you've marked -- you've marked them with two dots. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard Fadil Vishi, a Prosecution witness, and K31 a protected witness, also testify here; Fadil Vishi from the village of Dubrava, and K31 from the village of Reka. Vishi says that on the 25th of May, 1999 or thereabouts forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded and attacked the village. General, did your forces surround and attack the villages of Dubrava and Reka on the 25th of May -- on or about the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given the reasons why the units were not allowed to move from one area to another, carry out movements and manoeuvres, but had to stay at their positions. One of the positions is located here. That's the support artillery position. It's a unit to the south, and it was outside the built-up area. It had been there since the 23rd or 24th of March and it did not move until the end of the war, until the end of the campaign against Yugoslavia from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: These villages and their surroundings, were they terrorist strongholds?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely in this area at -- where these two roads separate towards Ljuborcice, Strpce, and so on, this was a very strong terrorist stronghold. In our estimation, this was the 162nd Terrorist Brigade there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did you provide support to the MUP in that area also?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, MUP did have conflicts at Hrasnica going from Uresnica [phoen] towards Globocica and Strpce. And in that fighting with the terrorists, the unit that was at the positions, that is, the artillery, took up the defence area from where fighting was conducted, which means this was to the north of their positions for a circular defence. If that support, then it was there, because it was defending its own positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the army leave its positions and enter these villages?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the army did not leave its positions, because it would have left the guns - that is, the cannons - unprotected if it had gone to search the villages or do anything else there. They had to stay by their artillery pieces. Artillery men know that have to be constantly near their artillery pieces and ammunition and projectiles. These are crews of six to seven men, not just one person that have to take care of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In view of the vicinity of the village, was it technically possible to target these villages from those positions?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, with these artillery pieces, from that position, or if we say hypothetically that they moved a few metres, which would not have meant anything, it would be impossible to target these villages because they would be firing on their own combat positions. It would have been so-called friendly fire, causing major casualties in our own ranks. Artillery is for support, and it fires at long ranges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were weapons confiscated from terrorists in the area?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several dozen weapons were confiscated. Dozens of long barrels were confiscated, rifles, ammunition for recoilless gun, several pistols. I don't remember now, but we reported regularly to the corps command about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these -- are these weapons confiscated by the -- by your men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were mainly confiscated by the MUP forces and some of the weapons were found near our positions, because fleeing from the MUP forces in fighting, they probably left behind some of their weapons. In the area around the firing positions, we found these weapons lying around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we dealing still, Mr. Cepic, with --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is in relation to -- to Dubrava and-- so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is still the -- this is still the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, about 25 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So on the 25th of May, you confiscated weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, some weapons. But weapons they had left behind. We didn't take it from them directly. These were weapons which we found in the area while searching the terrain after fighting to make sure that there were no terrorists left that might threaten the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this time you were involved in the clean-up operation, which in the past -- in previous examples you've said was done by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I may have expressed myself badly or it might have been misinterpreted. The unit was at its position. Some of the men were on duty. If in the immediate vicinity there is fire, fire is opened in the direction of the unit and its position, an alert is raised, the unit takes up positions for circular defence, which is not in the immediate vicinity of the artillery piece but some 50 or 100 metres away from it, to defend the artillery piece position. The soldiers sleep there, live there, dug in underground in dugouts. And as on that day, the MUP had carried out an action and was chasing terrorists from the north, from Hrasnica. After that shooting, the army took up those positions, and that is sort of static support from our own positions, defending positions we had taken up before the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English translation that we got was: "These were weapons which we found in the area while searching the terrain after fighting to make sure that there were no terrorists left that might threaten the unit." Now, that sounds like clearing up the terrain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clearing up the terrain is quite another concept. When there is organised fighting against terrorists in a built-up area, there's an entire methodology as to how clearing up of the training is carried out. This was not mopping up. This was, rather, inspecting the terrain. And around that area, when the terrain was searched, after all the fighting that the MUP had had with them, weapons -- some weapons were found in that area. So it was not mopping up the terrain in a built-up area or where the terrorists were. There was no strength or equipment for mopping up. These were Howitzer artillery pieces, which are static, and they engage in battle indirectly. They use large-calibre -- large calibres to support the forces in the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry. General, I have one clarification to make and to request you to kindly do it. You didn't have any infantry units around you or with you being the -- you being the artillery, you didn't have the infantry with you, did -- didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a tank man. This was a mechanised brigade. It was all on steel vehicles, tanks and armoured personnel carriers. Whereas, support pieces have to be pulled along. They don't have infantry with them. They just have crews manning the artillery pieces, various kinds of tasks are carried out by the crew that have to man that weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But it's not -- it's not only the tanks or the armoured corps which -- or the armoured division which has to solo -- take a solo action. The -- the infantry or the artillery units, aren't they attached to it for -- for accomplishing things on the ground? Weren't you equipped that way? Why -- why were you having a solo -- why were you conducting a solo action only with the tanks? And when you talk of these crew, there wouldn't be very many. They would only be to look after the tanks. But then what -- we couldn't -- I couldn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand the interpretation, tanks are not mentioned anywhere. These were only artillery pieces, Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... armoured unit, armoured vehicles. Sorry, I mixed up the terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no armoured units in the immediate vicinity. Armoured units have three or four members of the crew. Any member of the crew leaving the tank, well, that's a recipe for disaster. There was no organised legal action by us to support the MUP forces in the fight against terrorism. Rather, the unit was at its position, and on the north side the Ministry of the Interior, because of an ambush that had been set there, set out to search for terrorists. As this was in the area of these villages and the combat position was outside the built-up area, when the first round of bullets was fired, whether the unit had been attacked or not, that was a signal to take up defence positions. It was there simply as static support, conditionally speaking, to the MUP forces, because it had blocked that part that would lead to their positions. If you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, I'm confused now. Are you saying that -- that you did have tanks or you did not have tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have tanks in the brigade, but here on these positions there were no tanks. It was just Howitzers, ones that you have to pull along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just one more clarification. Did members of your unit in that area on that day in that period of time leave the area where the forces were deployed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that they did not and they could not for their own sakes. They could not leave the area where the artillery pieces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, how did they manage to search the territory to see if there were any remaining terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question. After the defence, when the fighting stops, when the danger is over, then scouts are designated, because the artillery also has scouts, just as the infantry does, and they tour the territory to make sure that there are no leftover groups that might threaten the unit. Because as you can see, this is all taking place in a very small area. And when searching the terrain in this way, they found equipment left behind by the terrorists. That is what is usually done after the fighting is over, not in the course of the fighting, because they would be exposing themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There is a Prosecution exhibit containing a map. I think it's P370. We did not ask for it to be shown, but if need be, to clarify matters further for the Bench, we can show that map to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It depends -- it depends what you're trying to clarify. I've got the answers I want. If ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence is satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the army inspect civilians' identity papers? Did they arrest them and take them outside the border belt?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the border belt and outside the combat deployment -- the combat disposition of the units, the unit -- the army was not authorised to inspect civilians' identity papers. That was a job for the MUP, and they were the only ones who could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I am sorry. You have to clarify here. Even if they were not authorised, were they doing it or they were not doing it? That's -- that's something important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army was not on the roads or in built-up areas, so it could not stop civilians and ask to see their identity papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is again a vague answer. You are under oath. Can you tell us whether they were doing it or not. That's important. I mean, this is just beating about the bush. It's a nice way of saying it, but please tell us whether they -- they did it or they didn't. What is your -- you're under testimony. You're under oath. You have to tell us the truth. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army did not check civilians' identity papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the army arrest civilians in the interior?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No arrests were made unless a crime was committed against a soldier or a military vehicle, and then that would have been done by the organs of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about within the border belt? Did they check civilians' identity papers there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the units inside the border belt, on the line and in-depth security, would check the identity papers of anybody caught in the area, and then that person would be further processed. That was only inside the border belt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You also made reference to "the combat deployment area." What -- what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The combat disposition or deployment area is the area of each particular unit marked with three points. For example, if we take any example, one of these three combat groups in the Globocica area, it would go to the right, to the left, and in-depth, and it would stay in that area and only army would be allowed in that area. Those would be places where the army has taken a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that they checked identity papers in that area also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If anyone entered the area. Because these were combat positions which were always secured. So if somebody came along and entered that area, that person would be checked. Also if anyone was caught on the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Fadil Vishi said that the army was in the Silkapor factory during the war. Is it correct that the army was in that factory during the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the army was not in the Silkapor factory during the war but it was in the north, in Doganovici but outside the village. There was a command post designated by the corps commander who was the only one who had the right to designate a command post for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, the same witness, Fadil Vishi, a Prosecution witness testified that 1 kilometre away he saw a convoy of civilians stopped by soldiers. In all fairness, he did not see the uniforms clearly. He said verbatim: "I could not clearly see the uniforms except for the fact that they were military." Now I'm interested in the following: According to the tables of visibility and simple logic, is it possible to discern military uniforms at a distance of 1 kilometre?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that distance, that's about 1.0007, a person can be recognized at a distance of 3 to 4 hundred metres, and that only when one is in one's prime. Beyond that, no. You can only recognize the general colour, red, blue, white, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In millimetres, how much is that in relation to 1 kilometre? What was the value?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1.0007. But in view of the distance and in view of optical deception, beyond a distance of 400 metres it is impossible to discern a uniform in a plane at that, and if there are no clouds and if all the other positions are favourable for observation, with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 5D666.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you now complete -- finished with the map which we have on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can give it an IC number now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Maybe. I'm sorry, maybe I will use in relation to some other places later on, but now in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to be much longer in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's time for our -- another break. Mr. Jelic, this time it will be for an hour. So would you again please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, before the break I would like to ask for longer examination. I was slower than I had planned to be. I will try to speed up. Could I please have a bit of additional time, because I asked for -- asked for four hours of direct examination for this witness, but this is one of the more important witnesses for our defence, and I would like to investigate a few more areas in relation to the crime base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have no problem with that. Mr. Cepic, you've got to make an assessment of which witnesses need to be presented to us at length in oral examination, but you will be conscious of the need to look closely at your plans for the later witnesses, whose details you have not required to give the -- in connection with any weekly list, and hopefully as we progress you will be able to fit as many in as possible by using means other than oral evidence for the whole of the presentation. So we'll adjourn now and resume at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Kamenova will be absent this afternoon for urgent personal reasons, and we have decided it's in the interests of justice to continue in her absence. It will only be for this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have on our screens Exhibit 5D666, please. Unfortunately, I think that we haven't got translation for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I presume you should proceed on the same basis in each of these cases, unless the Prosecution raise the matter and we have to adjudicate on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what is this document? And could you please read it out?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an original document from the command of the 243rd Motorised Brigade dated the 4th of May, 1999. It has to do with collecting information about Siptar terrorist forces. It's an order that is submitted as follows: "According to incomplete information, Siptar terrorist forces, up to 50 to 70 terrorists strong, are in the municipality of Vitina (the village of Slatina, the village of Sladovina and the village of Vrbin) and 100 to 150 terrorists in the municipality of Kacanik (village of Nika, village of Bicevac, village of Raka, and original of Dubrava). In relation to that, I hereby order." "In the area of responsibility of your unit, through everyday reconnaissance and observation collect information about the location, strength, and activity of the Siptar terrorist forces and notify thereof through regular combat reports. In case terrorists carry out combat activities towards your units, take action to protect personnel and material, technical resources, and notify thereof through interim reports."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Is your name at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this -- that is my -- it says my name above the signature, but it is Dragan Kolundzija, Chief of Staff, who signed on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Muharrem Dashi, testified before this Honourable Trial Chamber, and he said that on the 21st of May, 1999, or around that date, the forces of the FRY in Serbia encircled the village of Stagovo. Tell us, did you encircle the village of Stagovo on or about the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on that date, before that date, or after the date. The army never encircled or jeopardized that village, and it was not in the vicinity of that village at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there any terrorist forces in the area around this village?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the terrorist forces were in the area of the village of Stagovo, especially in the village of Stagovo itself and to the east of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the mentioned period, were there any attacks at your unit outside the village of Stagovo?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that were there were the closest units in the area of Stari Kacanik and Kamena Glava, and these units had frequent attacks coming from that area from the woods, between Stagovo and Kamena Glava, that is to say, across this area. Across the Nerodimka River. There were frequent attacks against members of the military -- or rather, the positions of these two units, the anti-armour detachment and the battalion that was at Kamena Glava.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you have any wounded soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting usually took place at night and it was characteristic of this unit that was attacking. It mostly attacked during the night. And a in few attacks, because there were frequent attacks, one of our soldiers was seriously wounded, and he later succumbed to those wounds and died.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I ask you once again, did the forces of the Army of Yugoslavia ever enter the village of Stagovo itself?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Members of my brigade never ever entered the village of Stagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether any terrorists got hurt in the fighting around Stagovo?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we received, mostly it was information about the MUP -- from the MUP forces that controlled the territory. But through personal insight at the positions that were in front of these two units, we saw that they entered minefields and got killed probably as they tried to approach combat resources. These were strike units, the two strongest units from the brigade, the armoured detachment and the armoured battalion, that were preparing for decisive defence. They had prepared their positions and practically they could not be approached, and several times we found parts of clothing and even weapons just in front of the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, I mentioned a few villages in the municipality of Kacanik from which, according to the indictment, deportations, persecutions, and murders took place. The villages I just mentioned, how far away are they? What is the distance among them?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very small map. The distance is 2 or 3 kilometres between the different villages and the diameter is about 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This locality that we mentioned just now, did that constitute a major stronghold of the terrorist forces?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is where a brigade was of the KLA that constantly threatened these roads and positions in particular, as well as crossroads of, of the roads going to the south of Urosevac towards Macedonia and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you about the concentration of terrorist forces for the entire area. Was it equally spread out, or were there stronger concentrations in the area of Kacanik and beyond that, perhaps the surrounding municipalities too?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strongest concentration of terrorist forces was precisely among these three roads that were to the south of Urosevac. And according to our intelligence, that is where practically there were two brigades of terrorists, to the left and to the right of these forces. And the -- there were practically no terrorist forces. Speaking in military terms, to the east and west there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, in your previous testimony today, you mentioned that people moved out of these villages and you mentioned that that was before the aggression and during the aggression. Could you please tell me what are the main reasons, to the best of your knowledge, for the fact that people moved out?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This moving out took place primarily among these roads to the south of Urosevac. For the most part, it was due to pressure, due to coerced mobilisation of the population, pressure for them to join the KLA. Then this area was also supposed to be cleaned of civilians in order to create a corridor for the easier passage of NATO land forces through this area, because that is the shortest route leading to the Kosovo Plateau from the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The villages that we mentioned just now, are they an obstacle for a land invasion if it were to take place from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These villages did not constitute an obstacle, because they had already been cleaned of their civilian population already. To put it simply, in military terms, they softened the terrain for a land invasion from the Republic of Macedonia. Had there been civilians, the situation would have been quite different. Probably there wouldn't have been that many NATO air-strikes in this area and there would have been less danger involved and it would have been easier to carry out defence had there been no coerced mobilisation and expulsion of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us, on the map, but very briefly, geographically, where is it possible to carry out a penetration from the Republic of Albania?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us the main roads and railroads. And due to the geographic terrain, could you tell us where a land operation can take place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: We cannot hear the witness. The first part of the answer is missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, you'll need to start that answer again, because you're speaking away from the microphone. It's okay now. Please -- please start again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this area, there are three main communication lines: The main one from the Republic of Macedonia is from Djeneral Jankovic via the Kacanik gorge, Kacanik, and then towards Urosevac. The second one is from Globocica via Doganovici again towards Urosevac, and the third one, it's an auxiliary axis, as we call it, was to the west of Vitina going towards Urosevac. The main communication line that the NATO forces would have taken most probably would be along the road from Djeneral Jankovic to Urosevac and then further on towards Pristina -- or rather, Gnjilane and towards the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you just draw this for us and explain very briefly what kind of a configuration there is there on the ground -- no, no, no, no. No, please, on the map.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The configuration of the terrain. You're a tank main, in terms of your own VS, so could you just explain this in terms of a land invasion.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the road to Urosevac, and then from Globocica, further on towards Urosevac again, and from Vitina, here, roughly this area, further on towards Urosevac, or you can also go towards Gnjilane and then to Pristina. The terrain is hilly, mountainous. It becomes accessible only down roads. The altitudes range from 600 to 1.000 metres. Armoured mechanised forces cannot move anywhere but down the roads. Outside the roads, it is only mechanised, motorised, infantry units that can move along. The heavy units can only negotiate roads. There are practically no other communication lines that can be taken. In the winter period, it is still covered with snow, so on these mountainous roads it is practically impossible to use combat resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where does the plain start?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plain, Malo Kosovo, starts from Nerodimka that goes to Lepenac -- or rather, starts from Doganovic. Doganovic, Stari Kacanik, and that is when the plain starts -- and that is practically where the plain of Kosovo starts, or rather, the plateau of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just put a circle around this part where the plain starts.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, as we are watching this map, we are going to look at the main road Djeneral Jankovic-Kacanik-Urosevac, to the left and right of that road. Was there any moving-out during the course of the war, and tell us what are the locations involved?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from these two roads that I mentioned here, leading from Macedonia, to the left and to the right, to the east and west, that is to say, from this part that I'm drawing on the map now and this other part - that's the west - practically no one moved out. If there were such cases, they were just sporadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what territories and municipalities were involved? I need it for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's part of the territory, and they're not exactly divided the way I drew it here. So it's part of Kacanik, that's the eastern part. Then Vitina, practically no one moved out. And part of the Strpce municipality and also Urosevac as a town. Invariably about 60 per cent of the population would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just mentioned Urosevac. Bajram Bucaliu was a witness who testified here. He's from Staro Selo in the territory of the municipality of Urosevac and he claims that the forces of the Army of Yugoslavia on the 2nd of April, 1999 surrounded Staro Selo. Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Staro Selo is just by the main road between Pristina and Djeneral Jankovic. There were no troops ever in the village. And to the south-east there was one unit, to the south-east of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What kind of activities were taken by the units in that period?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a period that I referred to just now, the critical period when the units dug in, camouflaged themselves, and prepared to defend themselves from aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, why did the army not take up positions in some village?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, the army does not take up built-up areas because it defends the territory, not towns and villages. It takes up positions that are appropriate for effective use in defence, and depending on the type of weapons that the unit has.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The same witness says that the army searched houses in the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army did not search the villages. In that period, they were only setting up their positions. The army is not authorised to carry out searches or to check people's IDs, and so on. That was forbidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Further on the same witness says that his passenger vehicle and truck were taken away from him without any kind of certificate and up to the day when he testified, they were not returned to him, although he had requested that. That is his assertion.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that particular case, but if the vehicle was taken away from him in a legal way, then legally a certificate was given. All the vehicles that were taken away, that were duty-bound to be involved in mobilisation, according to the mobilisation rule, a certificate, a document is issued for each and every individual vehicle. If that unit was anywhere in the army, he would have the right -- a right to exercise. And if he has such a document, to this day he can exercise all the rights belonging to him on the basis of law. If somebody took this away from him by violent means, he should have reported it to the Ministry of the Interior and then it is the Ministry of the Interior that is supposed to deal with a case like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you're a tank man. Witness Bucaliu alleges that there are some tanks in the village which did not have their barrels out. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's impossible. On every tank there is a -- there is a barrel fixed to the turret. It turns left and right, up and down through the stabiliser. It's not a small-calibre barrel that can be removed. You need a crane to lift it up out of the turret. So that would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Does the same witness -- the same witness says that the letters "VJ" could be seen on the caps of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not on the caps. There were no letter insignia on the caps. There were just the standard uniforms and insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The same witness alleges that paramilitary forces entered the village on the 15th of April, 1999 and blocked all exits from the village. Are you aware of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I didn't know about that. I don't know to this day whether that's how it was, except for what I hear now. There were no paramilitary forces in my unit. I don't exclude the possibility that there was some sort of inter-ethnic conflict, that the villagers settled accounts among themselves. But there were no paramilitary forces in the brigade. Everything was under the brigade command, all those who went to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the appearance and the uniforms, but he also says that these members who were in the Duge Brade [phoen] village had long hair and cockades. Would it be possible for a member of the army to have a long beard and a cockades?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the soldiers who were trained in those units were trained about personal hygiene, the manner of dressing, and you couldn't tell them apart from other soldiers, apart from what we've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to be more precise, could anyone have a long beard, long hair, or wear a cockade on their uniform?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's against the rules of service, and that would not pass muster on inspection, and I exclude the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The town of Urosevac. In the town itself, were there any combat forces during the aggression?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the combat units were in the defence areas. In the town of Urosevac, there were no such units, only the medical staff remained and an outpatients clinic for members of the army. There were hundreds of medical examinations of civilians as well, regardless of their ethnicity or religion. And you can see that in the clinic protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the army transport civilians at all and did it have the capacity to do so? From Urosevac, that is, and in general.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade did not have the capability to transport civilians. It could only transport men in connection with combat tasks, and it never dealt with the transport of civilians in any way. I don't exclude the possibility that a medical motor vehicle might have provided assistance to someone, but otherwise there was no transport of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, I have two questions about your evidence recently. You -- when you were dealing with Staro Selo, you said that the VJ did not ever enter Staro Selo. Was there a -- a MUP anti-terrorist operation there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period, as far as I know, no anti-terrorist action was carried out by the MUP. It might have been carried out in some other period of time, but in that period, to the best of my recollection, there was no such action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you said that if someone had his vehicle confiscated by the army without the appropriate procedure being followed, that should be reported to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand you. If somebody confiscated his vehicle forcibly, he would have had to report it to the Ministry of the Interior. We were not in Urosevac. We were not dealing with civilians or communicating with civilians, and there was no office where they could come and report this. Whether somebody took away his vehicle by force and whether that person was a civilian or a military person, he would have had to report that to the Ministry of the Interior and they would have to respond and we would cooperate with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If there was evidence to prove that the confiscation had been done illegally, who -- who would deal with the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is evidence that the army took it illegally, then the army would be responsible and it would have to compensate the person. That would relate to the truck as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there's no criminal offence related to seizing a -- a vehicle and seizing the documents of a private individual illegally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that if somebody took the vehicle without a receipt, if that's what they did, then they would certainly have to be held criminally responsible and answer to the authorities. And compensation for damages would always have to be provided by the institution, whether the Army of Yugoslavia or the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry. General, can you think of cases where compensation was in fact paid to people whose vehicles were taken away like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to confess. I was brigade commander. I didn't deal with that job. But there were several criminal reports filed against persons who illegally confiscated vehicles and other property, abusing their position or out of various interests. To the best of my knowledge, these persons have been prosecuted and they have been sentenced by the court in Nis. Some of this property has been restored or else compensation has been provided. I can't tell you what percentage was restored, but I'm sure it was 50 per cent or more, to the best of my recollection. But I no longer have access to these documents and I'm not in constant contact with those people, so I can't tell you more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: When did this happen? Much after the war was over or quite close to that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All criminal offences, if this relates to confiscated vehicles, we took criminal reports. And those persons were prosecuted immediately after the war. The biggest problem was where these persons were unknown. If these persons have not been detected to date, that's where the biggest problems are. But I'm sure that whenever it was discovered who it was that forcibly took property illegally, that person has been tried and the property either restored or compensation given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.
