utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A witness for the Prosecution, Florim Krasniqi, mentioned the village of Mirosavlje, and he said that he saw that on the 4th of April, 1999, from the direction of the village of Softovic, which is year this village, the villages of Orahovica and Zlatare were shelled, and that he learned that due to this shelling four persons were killed and five wounded in Zlatar. Is this correct, General? Was there shelling?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near Softovici [as interpreted] -- not in Softovici itself but near Softovici, there was a unit, but that unit could not target those villages, because they would also be firing on part of our forces. If you look at the map, you will see that part of the forces was in the vicinity of those villages, in their general area, not in the villages themselves. So in other words, had they done so, there would have been friendly fire. They would have been shooting on their own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the course of the war, how was technology used? I'm referring to artillery pieces and tanks.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used very restrictively during the war for well-known reasons. We were responding to attacks, to fire, and it was only permitted to open fire as a response to direct attacks on the positions and the units. There was a prohibition on the use of technical equipment for the reasons I have already mentioned, to avoid strikes by NATO, air-strikes by NATO. So technical equipment was used very restrictively in order to avoid revealing our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The same witness goes on to say that he heard that on the 5th of April, 1999, the army entered the village of Pojatiste and surrounding villages in tanks and that the soldiers searched houses in this village and expelled the civilian population from their houses.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in that period the army did not enter the village of Pojatiste and the surrounding villages because the army was already holding its positions with tanks as of the 24th of March. So neither did it enter the villages nor did it search houses or expel people. There was no reason to do that. The units were already at their position, and there was no reason to drive the tanks around. That would have been crazy, and who would have dared do it? Because the tanks would have been destroyed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the army enter the villages without tanks and search houses and expel civilians?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The army did not enter any of these villages or any villages at all. The army was engaged in dealing with its own problems, and those were problems of defence. So there was no expulsion from villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The same witness says that on the 7th of April, he saw fires in the distance and, according to what he said, it looked as if in the villages of Sojevo and Kamena Glava the houses were on fire. These villages, Sojevo and Kamena Glava, were they the target of any attack by the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those villages were never the target of an attack by the army, but if you look at the daily reports and interim reports which we sent, you will see that from the road, going from Urosevac towards Gnjilane, to the south, in the direction of Kamena Glava, on the section around the airport and those two main roads, these villages and these areas were targeted by NATO air-strikes almost daily. So it's quite likely that he saw fires, because we had huge fires, especially in Kamena Glava, caused by NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: He goes on to say that there was a military check-point near the village of Sojevo where there were M-84 tanks. Firstly, did you have M-84 tanks in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we did not. According to the Vienna Agreement and the controls, this was quite clearly visible. We had only T-55 tanks. Unfortunately we did not have M-84s, and we never set up any check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there any army check-points?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no army check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution witness, Bedri Hyseni, testified about the villages of Biba and Sojevo in the Urosevac municipality, saying that on the 29th of March, 1999, when the air-strikes began, two personnel carriers - he doesn't know whose they were, whether military or police - passed through villages of Biba and opened fire on the houses. Do you have any knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About opening fire, I don't have information about that. Probably they did pass through his village. Almost certainly they did, because that was D-day, when all the units left their barracks and went to take up positions. It's a bit strange that he says two, because it's usually three personnel carriers or tanks moving at a time. It's never two. But it's possible. It's possible that either the army or the MUP did pass through his village. But I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were they authorised to open fire?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not authorised to open any kind of fire. They would have revealed their whereabouts had they done so, and they would have been exposed to air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The same witness claims that the army had positions in the villages of Sojevo and Kamena Glava.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In tactical terms, the units were in the areas, not in the villages, especially at Kamena Glava. There's a road leading from Grlica towards Vitina. It's a key facility, and there one could prevent entry by NATO forces into Kosovo. There was an anti-armour detachment there, the two strongest units from the brigade were there, where the focus of defence was. There was no need for them to be inside the village, because under those mountainous conditions villages are unsuitable for defence. The villages are mainly in the valleys. The tactical facilities were on the heights. And from there one could fire on any possible aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All the means you had at those positions, all the weapons, and so on, were they camouflaged?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The first thing you do is camouflage when you take up positions after leading the barracks. After that, you fortify the positions and then you carry out additional camouflage for total protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The witness Hyseni claims that there were certain paramilitary formations in the villages of Biba and Sojevo and that they were led by a certain Novica Mijovic, from the village of Nekodim who worked in the army club in Urosevac and many people knew him. Are you aware of this and do you know that person? If you do know him, what do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first I have to say this: I don't know that there were paramilitary units there. If there were any, they were nowhere part of my brigade. There were no paramilitary formations. Secondly, Novica Mijovic is a civilian. He's over 54 or 55 years old. He worked in the Army Club of Yugoslavia. He had a heart operation, two bypasses, so he was given an easier job. Throughout the war, he worked in the Yugoslav Army Club. It's absurd to think that he could command some active units or some sort of paramilitary non-existent unit. Throughout this time, he was in the Yugoslav Army Club. I feel that these statements might be the result of some sort of settling of accounts among neighbours, but I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, what was the health condition of that man?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was ill. As I said, he had had a heart operation, with two bypasses. So physically he could not move around, let alone command a unit. I'm talking about the army, let alone the paramilitary. And he was employed in the Yugoslav Army Club all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness pointed out that he heard from other villagers that in the month of April allegedly the army had directed civilians to leave Sojevo and go to Urosevac. Did the army actually do that, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no expulsions. The army did not send anyone anywhere, from this village or anywhere else. They did not send anybody to the town of Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: During his testimony before this court, this witness pointed out that at the beginning of the war the house of his father-in-law in Urosevac was targeted from the barracks. Is that possible, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect, because when the war began, the army was on positions, all equipment, all personnel. Quite literally, the barracks were abandoned on the 24th of March. There was not a single person there to fire a single bullet. So it is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were the barracks in Urosevac targeted by NATO?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks were targeted several times, practically every day. According to our calculations, about 220 projectiles were fired at the barracks, and in total, in the area of responsibility of the brigade, over 400 projectiles. Those are our records and these reports we sent regularly to the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have on our screens Exhibit number 5D232, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am not clear about the situation at the barracks. Was anyone there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the barracks, when the war began, the 24th, all troops, literally, left the barracks. Everybody. In military terms, the barracks were abandoned. They took up positions for defence. No one stayed at barracks. No one. Quite literally, the barracks were abandoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who was counting the projectiles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our units -- or rather, the air defence units had observers and reconnaissance, and they were counting the projectiles, where they fell. Also, we had positions because the barracks in Urosevac are very characteristic. They are high above the town of Urosevac, about a kilometre away from Urosevac; that is to say, that nearby there are no residential houses except for the candy and biscuits factory Bambi. Even a layman could have counted the number of attacks and the number of projectiles. You can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have exhibit, as I said, 5D232, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what does this document represent, the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the command of the Pristina Corps, strictly confidential, the 28th of May, 1999, very urgent. It is sent to the 3rd Army Command and the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please just have a look at the last -- or rather, viewed from the end, the one-but-last bullet point and the one before that. What was targeted?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one but last?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The third one from the end.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From 2200 until 2400, 17 projectiles were fired at Staro Selo and Biba, the municipality of Urosevac. At 2315 hours, four missiles were fired at the Kacanik sector." And this last part does not pertain to my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are these the same villages that we referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Those that are a bit to the east and south of Urosevac. About a kilometre away and a bit more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit number 5D242, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, whose document is this?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the command of the Pristina Corps from the 24th of March, 1999 -- or rather, 24th of May, 1999. Could this please be blown up a bit, because I cannot see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this, 19-15, three missiles. What was targeted?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an interim operative report where it says -- oh, it went away. At 1915 hours with three missiles, a factory was targeted in Urosevac. There are many damaged houses in a radius of 300 to 500 metres around the factory."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you look at the other one that starts with the following words: "1945 with two missiles."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, the next one, the one after that.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just have it scrolled up a bit. Right. Thank you. "At 1945 hours, with two projectiles, Urosevac was hit, outside the town several projectiles no consequences."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How frequent were the bombings or Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Urosevac and the surrounding area were bombed practically every day. We have a report that we sent to the command of the Pristina Corps. On some days, incredibly enough there were even 50 missiles fired at Urosevac and the surrounding area in one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the village of Biljanica, the 31st of March, 1999. Prosecution witness Sefqet Zogaj and Hamide Fondaj say that an enormous number of Kosovo Albanians had fled to that locality, and they say that later they were forced to move away. My first question in this connection: Was there a major concentration of the KLA in that area?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to intelligence and as information was gathered, there were very strong concentrations of terrorist forces there, especially in the broader area of Malisevo. Our assessment was that there were about three brigades of terrorists there that had practically blocked the road from Dulje via the village of Blace to Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did your forces shell Belanica forcing displaced persons to flee toward the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never shelled the village of Belanica, and we did not force them to move towards Albania, because precisely this road, the one that I am talking about, it's the only one that goes via Suva Reka and further on to Albania. It's from my zone. And had we forced them to go, then we would have forcing them to go towards us, and that's absurd. It would have to be in the opposite direction, if that were so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you carry out any actions there?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An anti-terrorist action was carried out in order to deblock the road from the village of Blace to Gumcat, and that is roughly about a kilometre and a half to two kilometres from Belanica. That was part -- that was the task of part of the combat group that supported MUP activities. Further on, it was the MUP that was carrying out searches in the village and carrying out selections of the population as to who was a true civilian and who was engaged in combat and terrorist actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was the task of your combat group?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat group had the task of supporting MUP forces in breaking up terrorist forces, breaking up the blockade on the road to the village of Gumcat, and further on things developed according to--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end. There seemed to be further microphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about the area beyond Belanica?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never were civilians stopped in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: Could all microphones please be switched off in the courtroom except for the witness's -- or the speaker's, rather. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will have to repeat the question, because it's not recorded. Did your forces stop civilians? And even more specifically, did they have any contact with civilians in this area of Belanica?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no contact with civilians, and there weren't any civilians on this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system 5D659, please. I said 5D659. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your order?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my order, dated the 10th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is it that you're ordering in paragraph 1? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commanders of subordinated units should deal with perpetrators of crimes and other illegal acts. They must locate them on time and preferably isolate them. After that, they must get in touch with the chief of security of the 243rd Motorised Brigade" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see the text. What about the second paragraph? What does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This second paragraph -- well, if you don't want me to read it. It pertains to military conscripts and volunteers; that is to say, all members of the brigade, regardless of how they joined the brigade, the units. They should have the same status, rights, responsibilities, irrespective of the way in which they joined the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Were there any measures of checking your units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean inspection tours, as we say, control inspections, in military terms. Yes, there were several. We from the brigade command carried them out, and on average once in every 15 days we checked all positions, inspected all positions. Further on, the corps command sent regularly its own teams that toured units, and so did the army command. Often the corps commander and the army commander toured the units that were on positions. The person who was on these inspection tours for the longest period of time, it was the chief of the armoured and mechanised units, General Kovacevic, who was there most of the time. He was in Kosovo throughout the war and he spent most of his time in my unit, because his estimates and our estimates said that a possible land invasion would come from Macedonia and he was there to give us the benefit of his knowledge and his experience as the top organ in this field in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you tell me briefly whether any perpetrators were found, were any crimes committed in your unit, and were there any prosecutions, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there were no crimes committed by members of my brigade, or they were not discovered. All those that were discovered were prosecuted. Dozens -- or rather, tens were prosecuted before the courts during the war and later, after the war. I am not aware of the final outcome, and I cannot follow everything that's been going on, but all crimes that were committed, starting with ordinary theft, all of them were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We've already referred to the location of Djeneral Jankovic. That is also the name of a border crossing, a border post. Did the army have check-points there or at any other border crossings?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of the brigade, towards the border there were two border crossings and it was the customs officials and the border police that were these check-points. The army never carried out any checks at any border crossings. The closest military facilities were 1 kilometre away from the customs points.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did you ever receive from your superior, General Lazarevic, an order which would amount to a criminal offence, an order which would constitute a criminal offence if carried out?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No order from the corps commander, General Lazarevic, or anybody else from the Army of Yugoslavia arrived and was received by me which would amount to a crime. Had I received such an order, I would not have carried it out but I would immediately have informed the second superior. In the case of General Lazarevic, I would immediately have informed General Pavkovic, the army commander. That would have been my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Had you received an order the implementation of which would have amounted to a crime, would you have left any written trace of that in addition to informing the second supreme superior?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law and the regulators -- regulations, it would not be the superior officer who issued such an order who would be informed but his superior, and he would have to be informed in writing. And this was a method to prevent the issuing of orders which would amount to criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, General, I have completed my questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will give the map as further prepared an IC number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No Defence cross-examination? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and I appear for the Defence of General Sreten Lukic before this Tribunal. Our original intention was either not to cross-examine you at all or to cross-examine you very briefly. Today, however, issues have been raised we had not envisaged before, so you will have to devote some time to us in order for us to clarify certain points. Just a moment, please, if you can bear with me. Today when viewing Prosecution document P1972, which is a document where it says "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," dated the 14th of April, 1999, you said that along with this document there was an extract from the order of the Pristina Corps on a map pertaining to your brigade and also a plan of action for other units. We are now speaking of joint actions of the army and the police. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On these maps, were police units also entered?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police units are indicated differently on the map in two ways The first way is this: If they are acting in coordinated action as a neighbouring unit, then the police unit is drawn in separately and the army of the Yugoslavia unit is drawn in separately. If they are only providing support, then the police is marked in front and the Army of Yugoslavia is marked in behind. So there are two ways how these maps are made and how information is entered into them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If in the orders it says "in coordinated action with," then on the map these units should be drawn on the same line.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it should be. That's not to say that's how it was. It would depend on the context. But by definition, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what you said first, it was not always implemented, even though in the order it said that this was coordinated action, you would not always find the MUP units and the units of the VJ marked on the same line on the map.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say neither "yes" nor "no," because I don't see the document before me. I would need to see the map in order to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was a general one. You say that you cooperated with the chief of the SUP of Urosevac. How in your orders, were the MUP units reflected? For example, the PJP units. How did this come about?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that we cooperated with the chief of the Urosevac MUP, I meant to say that when I received a task or when he received a task, so whoever received the task first would call up the other one on the phone and tell him what was forthcoming. When one of us received a task or when we both received the task and had the documents, we would meet and see what the documents were about and what was supposed to be done in the forthcoming anti-terrorist action. Was that your question, or is there anything else you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll put some more questions to you about this. So then the two of you would discuss how the action could be carried out? Is that how it was? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would receive a decision from the commander of the Pristina Corps. In that order, the place, time, and targets would be defined. Sometimes even the means as to how this task should be carried out. The task I received, I would report on it to the corps commander, saying that I had received the task. If there was something I was not clear about, I would consult him. And then I would begin planning in the brigade, planning for the execution of the task. In the course of my planning, I would carry out coordination with the chief of the SUP. I don't know what his methods of work were in the MUP, but probably he was also making his plans, and we would coordinate this action in order to carry it out as successfully as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can we agree on this: The only plan made for an action is the plan made by you? The chief of the SUP doesn't make any kind of plan.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's absurd. I don't understand you. I receive a plan from the corps commander on which I base my plan. I receive an extract of his plan pertaining to my unit. In -- to me, that is an order, and I carry it out. In the MUP, what his forces will be, the size, composition, commander of those units, the security, the morale and psychological preparation, and so on, that is the job of the chief of the SUP, who is the only one competent to carry out those tasks. I wouldn't know how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that you know that the chief of SUP -- of the SUP made plans for the carrying out of the action?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only assuming that he needed to make plans. I don't know how or how detailed or what these plans looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see a single plan of that kind?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office of the chief of the SUP, I saw that several times. In particular, when he was in charge of the anti-terrorist action in Racak, they had plans, because before that he informed me of the plan he had received from his staff. I didn't have that plan, because I didn't need it. I didn't work on that. And secondly, at the command posts, when touring the command posts, because the combat group carrying out support for the MUP is not commanded by the brigade commander, just as the chief of SUP does not command these units at that level. So we would coordinate directly in those places, and there I would see plans on maps in the possession of company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was not referring to Racak. I think we started to talk about joint actions of the military and police.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. In other actions, also I saw the company commanders or company leaders, just as my commanders, the commanders of my units had my orders on maps and they issued their own orders, likewise I saw only a map. To be sure, I didn't see the text of the order. It was not within my competence to ask for those documents. But all the commanders of my units had to have all those documents before they set out to implement the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The maps you saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Lukic. I was only going to observe that this is very confusing. You're -- you're trying to focus the issue, but you're not getting answers directly to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. That's how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I was going to ask the witness to please listen carefully to the questions and answer directly the question you're being asked. And try and confine the answer to the particular subject, which is coordinated actions, not independent actions like Racak. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the maps you saw in the possession of members of the MUP and their commanders or company leaders, were these maps different from the military maps or were they military maps, extracts from military maps?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maps I saw looked like military maps. I did not analyse them. I didn't go into who published those maps, what the scale was, and so on. So I cannot confirm where those maps came from. They might have been copied. But I really cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today, when speaking about the zone or area of responsibility, you said that the overall situation was something you were responsible for when it comes to the combat disposition of the units. As for everything else outside the zone of defence, was the job of the civilian structures. Does that mean that you were not responsible for the situation in the zone of responsibility of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am responsible for the situation in the brigade areas. I had no authority to control a single municipality, a single infrastructure within it, the judiciary, the police, health care, all of which continued functioning and operating in the course of the war. I did not have the right to do that. All the municipalities in my zone were functioning - some better, some worse, depending on the situation on the ground - but not a single one was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the area of deployment of your units, in the zone of responsibility of your brigade, no other units were deployed? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No police forces were deployed there; is that correct? Except in the towns.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And the army was not in the towns at all, apart from the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come from that.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said "apart from the towns."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There were police in towns, is that correct, but not outside the towns. There were no police forces dislocated into the zone of responsibility of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were only temporary police stations or check-points, and I cannot really enumerate those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The check-points were on roads, not in the villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, mainly on roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Today you said that the security of the civilian population was the responsibility of the MUP; therefore, according to your testimony today, if there are civilians in the vicinity of your units in a village which is within the area of deployment of your units, in your view it's the police that is responsible for the security of the civilians in that village. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's partly true but not completely. I said that the units were not deployed in villages and towns. They were not deployed in built-up areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was coming to that. I wanted to come to that later on. But you answered a question put by my colleague, Mr. Cepic, and said that in towns there were no combat units. Were there any military territorial detachments in the towns, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military territorial detachments in my area of responsibility were not in towns. They received their areas, positions, and tasks and their main task was to protect facilities such as bridges, roads, repeaters, and there was one detachment in the far south of Kosovo in the Krivenik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw an order where a military territorial detachment was ordered to move out of a town, but we'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have in e-court Exhibit 5D1369. This was used during the examination-in-chief -- no, actually, no, no, it was rejected. I do apologise. But we can use 5D1285.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, this is a daily combat report, as we can see, issued by the command of the 243rd Motorised Brigade. In this document, in item 2.1, in the second paragraph, it says: "According to the decision of the 17th of April, 1999, parts of the brigade are engaged in blocking and scattering the Siptar terrorist forces. This action is still in progress."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see what action this part of your combat report refers?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see that from here, but that's an action, to the best of my recollection, carried out in Jezerske in blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this combat report of yours is incorrect. There's a mistake in the contents. Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying it's wrong. You pulled this out of context. I don't understand why it would be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, because it says that "parts of the brigade are engaged in blocking and dispersing, scattering, breaking up the Siptar terrorist forces."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so it was not just a blockade, as said. It was also crushing them. Well, as a rule, it was a blockade. But if the Siptar terrorist forces turned up, we would certainly engage in combat with them, combat to the death, because otherwise they would destroy us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that when it says in your combat report that your units participated in breaking up the Siptar terrorist forces, in the past tense, "participated in breaking them up," that they were only in blockade, that they were only blocking them?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that term can be interpreted in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you this - and we'll go village by village, the villages my colleague Mr. Cepic asked you about today - where you say that the army -- or rather, your unit in this particular instance, did not participate in anti-terrorist actions except, according to you, when these were carried out in the immediate vicinity of your units and you only took up circular defence positions and from that circular defence position you opened fire. We'll go through the documents. And this is one such document, which in our view, indicates that there was an active participation by units of the 243rd Motorised Brigade in the anti-terrorist actions. And now we'll move on. The Siptar terrorist forces, did they attack the positions where you were?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said several times that they attacked very, very often the positions and the columns that were on the move.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On these occasions, was there fighting between your units and the terrorist forces?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only natural that there was fighting at these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did these forces try to enter the FRY from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the positions were not at the border itself. They were in depth. In the interior of the territory. If they entered the territory, then it is certain that they fought with the units that were providing in-depth security of the state border or the area of defence, because the area of defence is not on the line itself but on tactical positions within the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is in-depth security. What about line security of the border? Did that exist?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Line security in war means that all units got the plan as to who they are subordinated to and then become part of combat groups, and these are actually areas of defence of battalions. In wartime, it was impossible to have units on the move through this line defence, because these people would be at risk. Their lives would be at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If members of your unit would get in contact with members of Siptar terrorist forces that were trying to enter the depth of the territory from Macedonia, in that case was there fighting with these forces?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably when you say "Siptar terrorist forces" you mean armed personnel, persons with weapons. Automatically, practically there would be a clash between our forces that were providing security or that were on positions, and these units that were spilling over from Macedonia into the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All these clashes were actually unplanned clashes; right? The ones that we mentioned until now. Clashes when terrorists attacked your units and clashes when terrorist forces tried to enter from Macedonia. These were clashes that had not been planned.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly were not planned. But what was planned was defence from forces that would possibly spill over from Macedonia and also an even more serious situation, if NATO forces were to be on the move, if there were to be a land invasion, ground invasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the following locations, are they in the area of responsibility of your brigade; namely, east, south, and north of Urosevac, Biba, Muhadzer Prelez, Raka, Staro Selo, Papaz, Varos Selo, and Mirosavlje. Are these villages in the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically all of these villages were in the area of responsibility of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Further on, the following locations in the Kacanik municipality: Kotlina, Ivaja, Stagovo, Slatina, Vata, Dubrava. What about them? Were they in the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that can be seen from the disposition of the unit that they were in the area of responsibility of the brigade or practically the areas that were taken up by the brigades. These were villages in the Kacanik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In response to the previous question, you said "almost all villages." When we were talking about localities in the Urosevac municipality, do you remember did I perhaps mention some that were not?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the north, whether it's Gnjilane or Urosevac. It's the border. But in principle, that's it. That's what the brigade practically covered, that part. That is why I said "practically all villages."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up in e-court 5D670.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is an order of the 243rd Motorised Brigade for carrying out combat activities. The date is the 22nd of May, 1999, and this exhibit was used today in this courtroom. In the first paragraph, it says: "On the basis of the order of the command of the Pristina Corps, dated the 21st of May, 1999, with a view to breaking up and crushing the remaining Siptar terrorist forces in the areas of deployment of the units, I hereby order." Let me ask you, first of all: In your view, was this order an order for passive or active activity on the part of military units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be passive if an order is issued to destroy terrorist forces. To be passive is just to stay put and do nothing, and everything else is active.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 5D662 on e-court. It was also used today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an order that has to do with protecting the civilian population, the command of the 243rd Motorised Brigade. And during your testimony today, you said that the protection of civilians is actually the concern of municipal authorities and it is not a duty on the part of combat units. They are assisted by the MUP too. Is it really your testimony here today that it is only the MUP -- or rather, the municipal authorities through the MUP that are responsible for the welfare of the civilian population, that the army has no responsibility in that? Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. For the welfare of the civilian population, these are our citizens and the army certainly has moral responsibility to help the civilian population in any way. But it does not primarily deal with that but, rather, the defence of the country in this period of time that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am talking about that time period. If it were peacetime, if there were no war, of course the welfare of the civilian population would only be in the hands of the police, because the army would be either in barracks or at the border.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the situation when the army is deployed in the territory in-depth, is there a responsibility on its shoulders as well for the welfare of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certain that the army also bears the responsibility for the civilian population on its shoulders, because it's our population. They're not strangers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you, because there is this order of the army to give assistance to the civilian population, and that remained unclear. Thank you. Now we talked about some actions and about the army not entering villages and the army not playing an active role. Rather, all actions were carried out by the police; whereas, the army was only giving support. It is the end of our working day and I'm just going to give you food for thought. But before that, tell me, did you issue an order on the 21st of March, 1999 for a blockade, breaking up and destroying of the Siptar terrorist forces in the broader area of Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 21st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall such an order. I do not see a document like that in front of me. There are quite a few orders, but every unit, when carrying out combat activities, had to have some order. At least, an order from the command of the brigade along with the approval of the superior command, because we had several orders to the effect that units could not move out of combat positions without previous approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It's the end of our working day. We will continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, that completes our sitting for today, which means that you will again have to return to give evidence, this time on Monday. Please remember what I said to you yesterday about how you treat the evidence in this case between now and your return. You must not discuss any aspect of the evidence of the case, past, present, or future, with anyone at all. Please concentrate on other matters over the weekend and return here refreshed, ready to resume your evidence at 9.00 on Monday morning. Now would you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is the possibility on Monday that the Chamber can sit on the same schedule as today, but that at the moment is not clear. The only thing that's definite for Monday is that we will sit in the morning and at least until 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry? Sorry, yes. Sorry. Until 1.45. But with the prospect of sitting until -- until 3.30. So we'll now adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of November, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.32 p.m.,
